chapters.title: Chapter XXIV
paragraphs: After three weeks I could leave my bedroom and move around the house. The first evening I was well enough to stay up, I asked Catherine to read to me, because my eyes were still weak. We were in the library, and the master had gone to bed. She agreed, though I thought she seemed reluctant. Supposing my books were not to her taste, I told her to choose anything she liked. She picked one of her favourites and read steadily for about an hour. Then the questions began.
“Ellen, aren't you tired? Wouldn't you be better off lying down now? You'll make yourself ill, staying up so long, Ellen.”
“No, no, dear, I'm not tired,” I kept answering.
When she saw that I would not move, she tried another way of showing how little she enjoyed her task. She began yawning and stretching, and then said—
“Ellen, I'm tired.”
“Stop reading, then, and talk to me,” I said.

That was worse. She fidgeted and sighed and kept checking her watch until eight. At last she went to her room, apparently quite overcome with sleep, judging by her heavy, irritable expression and the way she constantly rubbed her eyes. The next evening she was even more restless. On the third evening after I had rejoined her, she complained of a headache and left me. Her behaviour puzzled me. After sitting alone for a long time, I decided to see whether she felt better and invite her to lie on the sofa, instead of remaining upstairs in the dark. But Catherine was nowhere upstairs, or downstairs either. The servants said they had not seen her. I listened outside Mr. Edgar's door: everything was quiet. I went back to her room, put out my candle, and sat by the window.

The moon was bright, and a light dusting of snow covered the ground. Perhaps, I thought, she had taken it into her head to get some fresh air in the garden. I did see a figure slipping along the park's inner fence, but it was not my young mistress. When it came into the light, I recognised one of the grooms. He stood for some time watching the drive through the grounds, then suddenly hurried off as though he had spotted something. Soon he returned leading Miss Catherine's pony, with Catherine herself, just dismounted, walking beside it. The man quietly led the pony across the grass towards the stable. Cathy climbed through the drawing-room window and stole noiselessly upstairs to the room where I was waiting. She gently closed the door, slipped off her snowy shoes, and untied her hat. Still unaware that I was watching, she was taking off her cloak when I suddenly stood up and showed myself. For a moment the shock froze her. She made an inarticulate sound and stood perfectly still.

“My dear Miss Catherine,” I began, too mindful of her recent kindness to launch into a scolding, “where have you been riding at this time of night? And why did you try to deceive me with a story? Where have you been? Tell me!”
“To the bottom of the park,” she stammered. “I didn't tell you a story.”
“And nowhere else?” I insisted.
“No,” she muttered.

“Oh, Catherine!” I cried sadly. “You know you've been doing wrong, or you wouldn't be driven to lying to me. That really hurts me. I'd rather be ill for three months than hear you deliberately make up a lie.”
She rushed towards me, burst into tears, and flung her arms around my neck.
“Well, Ellen, I'm so frightened you'll be angry,” she said. “Promise you won't, and I'll tell you the whole truth. I hate keeping it hidden.”
We sat together on the window seat. I promised not to scold, whatever her secret was—though of course I had already guessed it—and she began.

“I've been going to Wuthering Heights, Ellen. Since you fell ill I've gone every day, except three times before you came downstairs and twice afterwards. I gave Michael books and pictures to have Minny ready every evening and put her back in the stable. Remember, you mustn't scold _him_ either. I reached the Heights by half past six, usually stayed until half past eight, and then galloped home. I didn't go just to enjoy myself. Often I was miserable the whole time. Now and then I was happy—perhaps once a week. At first I thought it would be terribly hard to persuade you to let me keep my promise to Linton: when we left him, I'd promised to visit again the next day. But you stayed upstairs that day, so I didn't have to persuade you. In the afternoon, while Michael was fixing the lock back onto the park gate, I got hold of the key. I told him my cousin wanted me to visit because he was ill and couldn't come to the Grange, and that papa would object to my going. Then I made an arrangement with him about the pony. He likes reading, and he's thinking of leaving soon to get married. He offered to do what I wanted if I lent him books from the library, but I preferred to give him my own, and he liked that even better.

“On my second visit Linton seemed quite cheerful. Zillah—their housekeeper—gave us a clean room and a good fire. She said Joseph was at a prayer meeting and Hareton Earnshaw was out with his dogs—stealing pheasants from our woods, I heard afterwards—so we could do as we pleased. She brought me warm wine and gingerbread and seemed wonderfully kind. Linton sat in the armchair, and I sat in the little rocking chair on the hearth. We laughed and talked so happily and found so much to say. We planned where we would go and what we would do in summer. I needn't repeat all that: you'd call it silly.

“But at one point we nearly quarrelled. He said the loveliest way to spend a hot July day was to lie from morning to evening on a bank of heather in the middle of the moors, with bees humming sleepily among the flowers, larks singing high overhead, and a blue sky and bright sun shining steadily without a cloud. That was his perfect idea of heavenly happiness. Mine was to sway in a rustling green tree, with a west wind blowing and brilliant white clouds racing above; and not just larks but thrushes, blackbirds, linnets, and cuckoos pouring out music everywhere. In the distance the moors would be broken by cool, shadowy valleys, and close by there would be great sweeps of long grass rolling in waves before the breeze, woods and the sound of water, and the whole world awake and wild with joy. He wanted everything to rest in an ecstasy of peace; I wanted everything to sparkle and dance in a glorious celebration. I said his heaven would be only half alive, and he said mine would be drunk. I said I'd fall asleep in his, and he said he couldn't breathe in mine, and grew quite snappish. At last we agreed to try both as soon as the weather was right. Then we kissed and made friends again.

“After sitting still for an hour, I looked at that big room with its smooth, bare floor and thought how lovely it would be to play there if we moved the table. I asked Linton to call Zillah to help us, and suggested blindman's buff, with her trying to catch us—you used to do that, Ellen, you know. He wouldn't. He said there was no fun in it, but he agreed to play ball with me. We found two balls in a cupboard among a heap of old toys: tops, hoops, battledores, and shuttlecocks. One had a C. on it, and the other an H. I wanted the C., for Catherine; the H. could stand for Heathcliff, his name. But the bran stuffing was coming out of H., and Linton didn't like that one. I kept beating him. He grew cross again, began coughing, and went back to his chair. That evening, though, it was easy to cheer him up. He loved two or three pretty songs I sang—_your_ songs, Ellen. When I had to leave, he begged and begged me to return the next evening, and I promised. Minny and I flew home as light as air, and all night I dreamt of Wuthering Heights and my sweet, darling cousin.

“The next day I was sad, partly because you were ill and partly because I wished my father knew about my visits and approved of them. But there was beautiful moonlight after tea, and as I rode along my gloom lifted. I'll have another happy evening, I thought, and what makes me happier still, my lovely Linton will too. I trotted up their garden and was turning towards the back when that fellow Earnshaw met me. He took my bridle and told me to go in at the front. He stroked Minny's neck, said she was a bonny beast, and seemed to want me to talk to him. I only told him to leave my horse alone or she would kick him. In his coarse accent he answered, ‘Wouldn't do much hurt if she did,’ and smiled as he looked at her legs. I was half tempted to make her try. But he moved away to open the door. As he lifted the latch, he looked up at the inscription above it and said, with a ridiculous mixture of awkwardness and pride, ‘Miss Catherine! I can read yon now.’
“‘How wonderful!’ I said. ‘Do let me hear you. You _have_ become clever!’
“He spelled out the name and laboured through it syllable by syllable: ‘Hareton Earnshaw.’
“‘And the numbers?’ I asked encouragingly, seeing that he had come to a complete stop.
“‘I can't make them out yet,’ he answered.
“‘Oh, you dunce!’ I said, laughing heartily at his failure.

“The fool stared at me, with something like a grin on his lips and a frown forming over his eyes. He seemed uncertain whether to laugh with me—whether I was being pleasantly familiar or showing what I really felt, contempt. I settled the question by suddenly becoming serious and telling him to go away: I'd come to see Linton, not him. He went red—I could see it in the moonlight—let go of the latch, and slunk away, the very picture of wounded vanity. I suppose he thought knowing how to spell his own name made him as accomplished as Linton, and he was terribly put out when I didn't agree.”

“Stop there, dear Miss Catherine!” I interrupted. “I won't scold you, but I don't like the way you behaved. If you'd remembered that Hareton is just as much your cousin as Master Heathcliff, you'd have realised how wrong it was. His wish to be as accomplished as Linton was at least something to admire. And he probably hadn't learnt just to show off. I've no doubt you'd already made him ashamed of his ignorance, and he wanted to improve himself and please you. Mocking his imperfect attempt was very ill-mannered. If _you_ had grown up as he did, would your manners be any better? As a child he was every bit as quick and intelligent as you, and it hurts me to see him despised now because that vile Heathcliff has treated him so unjustly.”

“Well, Ellen, you aren't going to cry over it, are you?” she exclaimed, surprised at how seriously I spoke. “But wait until you hear whether he learnt his ABC to please me, and whether the brute deserved any politeness. I went inside. Linton was lying on the settle and half rose to greet me.

“‘I'm ill tonight, Catherine, my love,’ he said. ‘You'll have to do all the talking and let me listen. Come and sit beside me. I knew you'd keep your promise, and I'll make you promise again before you leave.’

“Now I knew I mustn't tease him, because he was ill. I spoke gently, asked no questions, and took care not to irritate him at all. I'd brought some of my nicest books. He asked me to read a little from one, and I was just going to when Earnshaw burst through the door. Thinking things over had only made him angrier. He came straight up to us, grabbed Linton's arm, and swung him off the seat.
“‘Get to thy own room!’ he said, barely able to speak for rage, his face swollen and furious. ‘Take her there if she's come to see thee. Thou's not keeping me out of here. Off with ye, both of ye!’

“He swore at us and gave Linton no chance to answer, almost flinging him into the kitchen. As I followed he clenched his fist, looking as though he longed to knock me down. For a moment I was frightened and dropped one of the books. He kicked it after me and shut us out. I heard a spiteful, crackling laugh by the fire. Turning, I saw that hateful Joseph standing there, shaking and rubbing his bony hands.

“‘I knew he'd give ye what for! He's a grand lad! He's got t' right spirit in him! _He_ knows—aye, he knows as well as I do who ought to be t' master in there. Ech, ech, ech! He shifted ye sharp enough! Ech, ech, ech!’
“‘Where shall we go?’ I asked my cousin, ignoring the old wretch's jeering.

“Linton was pale and trembling. He wasn't pretty then, Ellen—oh, no! He looked dreadful. His thin face and large eyes were twisted with frantic, helpless fury. He seized the door handle and shook it, but the door was locked from inside.
“‘Let me in or I'll kill you! Let me in or I'll kill you!’ he screamed, rather than spoke. ‘Devil! Devil! I'll kill you—I'll kill you!’
“Joseph gave another croaking laugh.
“‘There, that's his father!’ he cried. ‘That's his father! We've always summat from each side in us. Never mind, Hareton, lad—don't thee be frightened. He can't get at thee!’

“I caught Linton's hands and tried to pull him away, but he screamed so terribly that I dared not go on. At last a dreadful coughing fit choked off his cries. Blood poured from his mouth, and he fell to the floor. Sick with terror, I ran into the yard and shouted for Zillah as loudly as I could. She soon heard me. She was milking the cows in a shed behind the barn and came hurrying to ask what was wrong. I couldn't catch my breath to explain. I dragged her inside and looked around for Linton. Earnshaw had come out to see what harm he'd done, and was carrying the poor boy upstairs. Zillah and I followed, but at the top of the stairs he stopped me and said I couldn't go in: I must go home. I cried out that he'd killed Linton and that I _would_ go in. Joseph locked the door and said I'd do ‘nowt of t' sort,’ and asked whether I was ‘going to be as mad as him.’ I stood there crying until the housekeeper came back. She said he'd be better in a little while, but couldn't bear all that shrieking and noise. Then she took hold of me and almost carried me downstairs into the main room.

“Ellen, I could have torn my hair out! I sobbed and cried until I could hardly see. And the ruffian you feel so sorry for stood opposite me, taking it upon himself every now and then to tell me to ‘hush,’ and saying it wasn't his fault. Finally my threats to tell papa and have him put in prison and hanged frightened him into blubbering too. He hurried out to hide his cowardly distress. But even then I hadn't seen the last of him. When at last they made me leave and I was a few hundred yards from the house, he suddenly stepped out of the shadows beside the road, stopped Minny, and caught hold of me.
“‘Miss Catherine, I'm sorely grieved,’ he began, ‘but it's rather too bad—’
“I struck him with my whip, thinking he might murder me. He let go, roaring one of his dreadful curses, and I galloped home almost out of my mind.

“I didn't say good night to you that evening, and the next day I didn't go to Wuthering Heights. I wanted to terribly, but I was in a strange, agitated state. One moment I dreaded hearing that Linton was dead; the next I shuddered at the thought of meeting Hareton. On the third day I found courage—or at least I couldn't bear the uncertainty any longer—and slipped away again. I went at five, on foot, thinking I might creep into the house and up to Linton's room without being seen. But the dogs announced me. Zillah welcomed me, said ‘the lad was getting on nicely,’ and took me into a small, neat, carpeted room. To my indescribable joy, there was Linton on a little sofa, reading one of my books. But for an entire hour he wouldn't speak to me or even look at me, Ellen. He has such a miserable temper. And what utterly astonished me was that when he finally spoke, he told the lie that _I_ had caused the trouble and Hareton wasn't to blame! I couldn't answer without losing my temper, so I got up and left. He called a faint ‘Catherine!’ after me. He hadn't expected me to react like that, but I wouldn't go back. The following day was the second time I stayed home, almost determined never to visit him again. Yet it was so wretched to go to bed and get up without hearing anything about him that my resolve vanished before I'd properly formed it. Once, making the journey _had_ seemed wrong; now staying away seemed wrong. Michael came to ask whether he should saddle Minny. I said yes, and as she carried me over the hills I felt I was doing my duty. To reach the yard I had to pass the front windows, so there was no point trying to hide my arrival.

“‘Young master's in the main room,’ Zillah said when she saw me heading for the parlour. I went in. Earnshaw was there too, but left at once. Linton was sitting half asleep in the big armchair. I walked up to the fire and began seriously, partly meaning what I said—

“‘Since you don't like me, Linton, and think I come here deliberately to hurt you—and claim that's what I do every time—this is our last visit. Let's say goodbye. Tell Mr. Heathcliff you don't want to see me, and he must stop making up lies about it.’

“‘Sit down and take off your hat, Catherine,’ he answered. ‘You're so much happier than I am that you ought to be better too. Papa talks about my faults enough, and shows enough contempt for me, to make it natural for me to doubt myself. I often wonder whether I'm just as worthless as he says. Then I feel so angry and bitter that I hate everyone! I _am_ worthless, bad-tempered and mean-spirited, almost all the time. And if you choose, you _can_ say goodbye: you'll be getting rid of a nuisance. Only, Catherine, be fair to me in this one thing. Believe that if I could be as sweet, as kind, and as good as you, I would choose that as readily as being happy and healthy—more readily, even. And believe that your kindness has made me love you more deeply than I would if I deserved your love. Though I couldn't help showing you what I'm like, and still can't, I regret it and I'm sorry for it. I shall regret it and be sorry until I die!’

“I felt he was telling the truth, and that I had to forgive him. Even if we quarrelled the next minute, I'd have to forgive him again. We made peace, but we both cried the whole time I stayed. It wasn't entirely from sadness, though I _was_ sad that Linton's nature was so twisted. He'll never let his friends be comfortable, and he'll never be comfortable himself! Since that evening I've always gone to his little parlour, because his father came back the day afterwards.

“About three times, I think, we've been as happy and hopeful as we were that first evening. All my other visits have been gloomy and troubled, sometimes by his selfishness and spite, sometimes by his suffering. But I've learnt to bear the first almost as patiently as the second. Mr. Heathcliff keeps out of my way on purpose; I've hardly seen him. Last Sunday, though, I arrived earlier than usual and heard him cruelly abusing poor Linton for how he'd behaved the evening before. I don't know how he knew about it, unless he'd been listening. Linton certainly had been provoking, but that was nobody's business except mine. I interrupted Mr. Heathcliff's lecture by walking in and telling him so. He burst out laughing and went away, saying he was glad I saw it that way. Since then I've told Linton he must whisper his bitter remarks. Now, Ellen, you've heard everything. You can't stop me going to Wuthering Heights without making two people miserable. But if you just don't tell papa, my visits needn't disturb anyone's peace. You won't tell him, will you? It would be very heartless if you did.”
“I'll decide that by tomorrow, Miss Catherine,” I replied. “It needs some thought, so I'll leave you to rest and go and consider it.”

I considered it aloud in my master's presence, going straight from her room to his and telling him the whole story, except for her conversations with her cousin and anything about Hareton. Mr. Linton was more alarmed and distressed than he would admit to me. In the morning Catherine discovered that I had betrayed her confidence, and that her secret visits were forbidden. She wept and struggled against the ban, begging her father to pity Linton, but it was no use. Her only consolation was his promise to write to Linton and invite him to the Grange whenever he pleased, while explaining that he could no longer expect Catherine to visit Wuthering Heights. Had he known his nephew's character and state of health, perhaps he would have thought it better to deny even that small comfort.

chapters.title: Chapter XXV
paragraphs: “All this happened last winter, sir,” said Mrs. Dean, “scarcely more than a year ago. Last winter I never imagined that twelve months later I'd be entertaining a stranger to the family by telling him about it! Still, who knows how long you'll remain a stranger? You're too young to be content with living alone for ever, and somehow I don't think anyone could see Catherine Linton without loving her. You smile—but why do you look so animated and interested whenever I talk about her? Why have you asked me to put her portrait above your fireplace? And why—?”

“Enough, my good friend!” I cried. “It's quite possible that _I_ could love her, but would she love me? I'm too doubtful of that to risk my peace of mind by exposing myself to temptation. Besides, this isn't my home. I belong to the busy world, and I must return to its embrace. Go on. Did Catherine obey her father?”

“She did,” the housekeeper continued. “Her love for him was still the strongest feeling in her heart. And he spoke without anger, with the deep tenderness of someone about to leave his greatest treasure among dangers and enemies, knowing that the memory of his words would be the only help he could leave to guide her. A few days later he said to me, ‘I wish my nephew would write, Ellen, or come to visit. Tell me honestly what you think of him. Has he improved, or is there any hope that he will as he grows into a man?’

“‘He's very frail, sir,’ I replied, ‘and hardly likely to live to manhood. But I can say this: he isn't like his father. If Miss Catherine were unfortunate enough to marry him, she could manage him, unless she foolishly indulged him far too much. Still, master, you'll have plenty of time to get to know him and decide whether he would suit her. He won't come of age for another four years or more.’”

Edgar sighed and went to the window, looking out towards Gimmerton church. The afternoon was misty, but the February sun shone faintly, and we could just make out the two fir trees in the churchyard and the scattered gravestones.

“I've often prayed,” he said, almost to himself, “for what's approaching now. And now I begin to shrink from it and feel afraid. I thought the memory of coming down that valley as a bridegroom would be less sweet than the thought of being carried back up it in a few months, perhaps only weeks, and laid in its lonely hollow! Ellen, I've been very happy with my little Cathy. Through winter nights and summer days, she has been a living hope beside me. Yet I've been just as happy thinking alone among those stones beneath the old church, lying through the long June evenings on the green mound of her mother's grave, wishing—aching—for the time when I could lie underneath it. What can I do for Cathy? How can I leave her? I wouldn't care for a moment that Linton was Heathcliff's son, or that he took her away from me, if he could comfort her when she lost me. I wouldn't care if Heathcliff got what he wanted and triumphed in robbing me of my last blessing! But if Linton is unworthy—if he's only his father's feeble tool—I can't abandon her to him. However hard it is to crush her happy spirit, I must go on making her sad while I live and leave her alone when I die. My darling! I'd rather give her up to God and lay her in the earth before me.”

“Entrust her to God now, sir,” I answered. “And if we should lose you—God forbid it—with His help I'll remain her friend and adviser to the end. Miss Catherine is a good girl. I'm not afraid she'll knowingly do wrong, and people who do their duty are always rewarded in the end.”

Spring moved on, but my master gained no real strength, though he began walking in the grounds with his daughter again. In her inexperience, she took this alone as proof that he was recovering. His cheeks were often flushed too, and his eyes bright, so she felt certain he would get well. On her seventeenth birthday he did not go to the churchyard. It was raining, and I said—
“Surely you won't go out tonight, sir?”
“No,” he answered. “This year I'll put it off a little longer.”

He wrote to Linton again, saying how much he wished to see him. Had the sick boy been fit to be seen, I have no doubt his father would have let him come. As it was, Linton replied as he had been instructed: Mr. Heathcliff objected to his visiting the Grange, but his uncle's kind concern delighted him. He hoped they might sometimes meet on his uncle's walks, when he could ask him in person not to keep him and his cousin so completely apart much longer.
That part of the letter was straightforward and probably his own. Heathcliff knew that by now he could plead eloquently for Catherine's company.

“I'm not asking,” he wrote, “for her to visit me here. But am I never to see her, because my father won't let me go to her home and you won't let her come to mine? Please ride with her towards the Heights now and then, and let us talk for a few minutes in front of you! We've done nothing to deserve being separated, and you're not angry with me. You admit yourself that you have no reason to dislike me. Dear uncle, send me a kind note tomorrow, and permission to meet you anywhere you choose except Thrushcross Grange. I believe that if we met, you'd be convinced that I don't have my father's character. He says I'm more your nephew than his son. Though I have faults that make me unworthy of Catherine, she has forgiven them, and for her sake you should too. You ask about my health. It has improved, but how can I be cheerful and well when I have no hope, and am condemned to be alone or with people who have never liked me and never will?”

Edgar felt sorry for the boy, but could not agree, since he could not accompany Catherine. Perhaps they might meet in summer, he said. Meanwhile he wanted Linton to keep writing occasionally, and promised to offer whatever advice and comfort he could by letter, knowing how hard the boy's position in his family was. Linton did as he asked. Left to himself, he would probably have ruined everything by filling his letters with complaints and lamentations. But his father watched him closely, and of course insisted on seeing every line my master sent. So instead of writing about his own particular sufferings and troubles—the things always uppermost in his mind—he kept returning to the cruelty of being forced apart from his friend and love. He gently suggested that Mr. Linton must soon let them meet, or he would begin to fear that his uncle was deliberately deceiving him with empty promises.

At home Cathy was a powerful ally. Between them they eventually persuaded my master to allow them a ride or a walk together about once a week, under my supervision, on the moors closest to the Grange. By June his health was still declining. Although he had set aside part of his income each year for my young mistress's inheritance, he naturally wanted her to keep her ancestral home—or at least return to it before long. He thought her only chance of doing so was to marry his heir. He had no idea that the boy was deteriorating almost as fast as he was himself, and I believe no one else knew either. No doctor visited the Heights, and none of us saw young Master Heathcliff to bring back news of his condition. For my part, I began to think my fears had been mistaken and that he really must be recovering, since he spoke of riding and walking on the moors and seemed so intent on getting what he wanted. I could not imagine a father treating a dying child with the tyranny and wickedness that, as I later learnt, Heathcliff used to force this apparent eagerness out of him. The more immediately death threatened to defeat his greedy, heartless plans, the harder he drove the boy.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVI
paragraphs: Summer was already past its height when Edgar reluctantly gave in to their pleas, and Catherine and I set out on our first ride to meet her cousin. The day was close and sultry, without sunshine, though the sky was too hazy and mottled to promise rain. We had agreed to meet at the guidepost by the crossroads. But when we arrived, a little herd-boy sent to meet us said, “Master Linton's just this side o' t' Heights, and he'd be much obliged if ye'd come a bit further.”
“Then Master Linton has forgotten his uncle's very first instruction,” I said. “He told us to stay on Grange land, and we're leaving it already.”
“Well, once we reach him we'll turn the horses towards home,” my companion answered. “That's the direction we'll take for our ride.”

But when we found him, scarcely a quarter of a mile from his own door, he had no horse. We had to dismount and let ours graze. He was lying on the heather waiting for us, and did not get up until we were only a few yards away. His steps were so weak and his face so pale that I exclaimed at once, “Why, Master Heathcliff, you're in no state to enjoy a walk this morning. How ill you look!”

Catherine looked at him in sorrow and astonishment. The joyful greeting on her lips became a cry of alarm, and instead of celebrating their long-delayed meeting she anxiously asked whether he was worse than usual.

“No—better—better!” he gasped, trembling and holding on to her hand as though he needed it to support him. His large blue eyes moved timidly over her. The hollows around them had changed their once languid expression into something haggard and wild.
“But you have been worse,” his cousin insisted. “Worse than when I last saw you. You're thinner, and—”
“I'm tired,” he interrupted quickly. “It's too hot to walk. Let's rest here. And I often feel sick in the mornings. Papa says it's because I'm growing so fast.”
Far from reassured, Cathy sat down, and he lay beside her.

“This is rather like your paradise,” she said, trying to sound cheerful. “Do you remember the two days we agreed to spend in the places and ways each of us liked best? This is almost your day, except for the clouds. But they're so soft and gentle that it's nicer than sunshine. Next week, if you're able, we'll ride down to the Grange park and try mine.”

Linton did not seem to remember what she meant, and clearly found any sort of conversation a great effort. His indifference to the subjects she raised, and his complete inability to offer anything to entertain her, were so obvious that she could not hide her disappointment. Some indefinable change had come over his whole appearance and manner. The petulance that affection could turn to tenderness had given way to listless apathy. He seemed less like an irritable child who frets and teases to be comforted, and more like a chronic invalid, sullenly absorbed in himself, rejecting comfort and ready to take anyone else's cheerful laughter as an insult. Catherine saw as clearly as I did that he found our company more of a punishment than a pleasure, and before long she freely suggested leaving. Unexpectedly, the suggestion roused him from his lethargy and made him strangely agitated. He glanced towards the Heights in fear and begged her to stay at least another half-hour.

“But I think you'd be more comfortable at home than sitting here,” Cathy said. “I can see my stories and songs and chatter aren't amusing you today. You've grown wiser than I have in these six months; you don't much care for my amusements now. If I could entertain you, I'd gladly stay.”

“Stay and rest yourself,” he replied. “And, Catherine, don't think or say I'm _very_ ill. It's the muggy weather and the heat that make me so dull. And before you came I walked about quite a lot—for me. Tell uncle I'm fairly well, will you?”
“I'll tell him _you_ say so, Linton. I couldn't tell him you are,” my young mistress said, puzzled that he kept insisting on something so plainly untrue.

“And come back here next Thursday,” he went on, avoiding her bewildered eyes. “Thank him for letting you come—thank him very much, Catherine. And—and if you _did_ happen to meet my father and he asked about me, don't let him think I've been terribly quiet and stupid. Don't look sad and downhearted the way you _are_ looking. He'll be angry.”
“I don't care if he's angry,” Cathy cried, thinking his anger would be directed at her.
“But I do,” her cousin said with a shudder. “_Don't_ turn him against me, Catherine. He's very harsh.”
“Does he treat you harshly, Master Heathcliff?” I asked. “Has he tired of indulging you and begun to act on his hatred, instead of merely feeling it?”

Linton looked at me without answering. Cathy stayed beside him another ten minutes. His head drooped sleepily onto his chest, and he made no sound except muffled groans of exhaustion or pain. Then she tried to find some consolation in gathering bilberries and sharing her finds with me. She offered him none, seeing that any further attention would only tire and annoy him.
“Has it been half an hour yet, Ellen?” she whispered in my ear at last. “I don't know why we're staying. He's asleep, and papa will want us home.”
“Well, we can't leave him sleeping,” I answered. “Be patient and wait until he wakes. You were so eager to set out, but your longing to see poor Linton has worn off quickly enough!”

“Why did _he_ want to see me?” Catherine replied. “I liked him better in his worst tempers before than I do in this strange mood. It's as though seeing us were a task he's being forced to do for fear his father will scold him. But I'm certainly not coming here to please Mr. Heathcliff, whatever reason he has for making Linton go through this punishment. And although I'm glad his health is better, I'm sorry he's so much less pleasant and so much less affectionate towards me.”
“So you think his health _has_ improved?” I said.
“Yes,” she answered. “You know how he always made so much of his suffering. He's not fairly well, as he wanted me to tell papa, but he's probably better.”
“I don't agree with you there, Miss Cathy,” I said. “I should think he's much worse.”
At that moment Linton woke with a start, bewildered and terrified, and asked whether someone had called his name.
“No,” Catherine said, “unless it was in your dreams. I don't understand how you can fall asleep outdoors in the morning.”
“I thought I heard my father,” he gasped, looking up at the dark, overhanging crag above us. “Are you sure no one spoke?”

“Quite sure,” his cousin replied. “Ellen and I were only disagreeing about your health. Are you really stronger than when we last met in winter, Linton? If you are, there's one thing I'm certain hasn't grown stronger: your affection for me. Tell me—are you?”
Tears streamed from Linton's eyes as he answered, “Yes, yes, I am!” Still gripped by the voice he had imagined, he kept looking up and down for the person it belonged to.

Cathy stood up. “We must say goodbye for today,” she said. “I won't pretend I haven't been terribly disappointed by our meeting, though I won't tell anyone but you. That's not because I'm afraid of Mr. Heathcliff.”

“Hush!” Linton murmured. “For God's sake, hush! He's coming.” He clung to Catherine's arm, trying to hold her back, but at those words she quickly pulled free and whistled to Minny, who came to her like a dog.
“I'll be here next Thursday,” she called, springing into the saddle. “Goodbye. Hurry, Ellen!”
And so we left him. He was hardly aware that we were going, so completely was he occupied by the thought of his father's approach.

Before we reached home, Catherine's annoyance had softened into a confused mixture of pity and regret, mingled with vague, uneasy doubts about Linton's real condition, both in his health and his life at home. I shared those doubts, but advised her to say little: another visit would help us judge better. My master asked how our outing had gone. We duly passed on his nephew's thanks, and Miss Cathy touched lightly on the rest. My answers gave him little more information, for I hardly knew what I should conceal and what I should reveal.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVII
paragraphs: Seven days slipped by, each bringing a further, now rapid change in Edgar Linton's condition. The damage that once took months was now being done in hours. We would gladly have kept Catherine deceived, but her own quick understanding would not let her deceive herself. In secret she guessed at the dreadful likelihood and dwelt on it as it gradually became a certainty. When Thursday came she had no heart to mention her ride. I mentioned it for her and got permission to insist on her going outdoors. Her whole world had become her father's bedroom and the library, where he spent the short time each day that he could bear to sit up. She resented every moment not spent bending over his pillow or sitting beside him. Watching and sorrow had made her pale. My master willingly sent her out for what he hoped would be a happy change of scene and company, comforting himself with the thought that after his death she would not be entirely alone.

From several remarks he let fall, I gathered he had firmly persuaded himself that, since his nephew resembled him in looks, their minds would be alike too. Linton's letters gave little or no sign of his flawed character. Out of an excusable weakness, I did not correct the mistake. What good, I asked myself, would it do to trouble his last moments with knowledge he had neither the strength nor the opportunity to act upon?

We put off our outing until the afternoon—a golden August afternoon. Every breath of air from the hills seemed so full of life that anyone who breathed it, even someone dying, might revive. Catherine's face was like the landscape: sunshine and shadow passed over it in quick succession, but the shadows stayed longer and the sunshine faded sooner. Even that brief forgetting of her troubles made her poor little heart reproach itself.

We saw Linton waiting at the same place as before. My young mistress dismounted and told me that, as she meant to stay only a very short time, I had better remain on horseback and hold her pony. I refused. I would not risk letting the girl in my care out of my sight for a minute, so we climbed the heather slope together. This time Master Heathcliff greeted us with more animation, but it was neither high spirits nor happiness. It looked more like fear.
“You're late!” he said, struggling to get the short words out. “Isn't your father very ill? I thought you wouldn't come.”

“_Why_ can't you be honest?” cried Catherine, holding back her greeting. “Why not simply say you don't want me? It's strange, Linton: this is the second time you've deliberately brought me here, apparently for no reason except to upset us both!”
Linton shuddered and looked at her, half pleading, half ashamed. But his cousin had too little patience to put up with such baffling behaviour.

“My father _is_ very ill,” she said, “so why am I being called away from his bedside? If you didn't want me to keep my promise, why didn't you send word to release me from it? Come, explain yourself! I've no thought for games or nonsense now, and I can't spend my time attending to your affectations!”

“My affectations?” he murmured. “What do you mean? For heaven's sake, Catherine, don't look so angry! Despise me as much as you like. I'm a worthless, cowardly wretch, and no one could despise me enough. But I'm too contemptible to deserve your anger. Hate my father; keep only your contempt for me.”

“Nonsense!” Catherine cried furiously. “You foolish, silly boy! And look at him trembling, as though I were really going to touch him! You needn't ask for contempt, Linton. Anyone will give you that without being asked. Let go! I'm going home. It's ridiculous dragging you away from the fireside and pretending—what are we pretending? Let go of my dress! If I pitied you for crying and looking so frightened, you ought to reject such pity. Ellen, tell him how shameful this is. Get up! Don't lower yourself into a grovelling reptile—_don't_!”
With tears pouring down his face and agony in his expression, Linton had flung his powerless body along the ground. He seemed to be shaking with unbearable terror.

“Oh!” he sobbed. “I can't bear it! Catherine, Catherine, I'm a traitor too, and I daren't tell you! But if you leave me, I'll be killed! _Dear_ Catherine, my life is in your hands. You've said you love me, and if you did it, it wouldn't hurt you. You won't go, then? Kind, sweet, good Catherine! Perhaps you _will_ agree—and he'll let me die with you!”
Seeing his terrible distress, my young mistress bent to lift him. Her old, indulgent tenderness overcame her irritation, and she was deeply moved and frightened.

“Agree to what?” she asked. “To stay? Tell me what this strange talk means, and I will. You keep contradicting yourself, and you're driving me distracted! Calm down, be honest, and tell me at once everything that's troubling you. You wouldn't hurt me, would you, Linton? You wouldn't let an enemy harm me if you could stop them? I can believe you'd be a coward where you're concerned, but not a coward who betrays his best friend.”
“But my father threatened me,” the boy gasped, clasping his wasted fingers. “I'm terrified of him—terrified! I _daren't_ tell!”
“Oh, very well!” Catherine said with scornful pity. “Keep your secret. _I'm_ not a coward. Save yourself. I'm not afraid!”

Her generosity brought on fresh tears. He sobbed wildly and kissed the hands supporting him, yet still could not find the courage to speak plainly. I was wondering what lay behind all this, determined that Catherine should never suffer for his benefit or anyone else's if I could help it, when I heard a rustle in the heather. Looking up, I saw Mr. Heathcliff coming down from the Heights, almost upon us. He did not glance at my companions, though they were close enough for him to hear Linton sobbing. Instead he greeted me in the almost friendly tone he used with no one else, and whose sincerity I could never quite trust.

“It's something to find you so near my house, Nelly. How are things at the Grange? Tell me. The rumour is,” he added more quietly, “that Edgar Linton is on his deathbed. Perhaps they exaggerate how ill he is?”
“No, my master is dying,” I answered. “That's true enough. It will be a sad thing for us all, but a blessing for him!”
“How long do you think he'll last?” he asked.
“I don't know,” I replied.

“Because,” he continued, looking at the two young people, who froze under his gaze—Linton seemed afraid even to move or lift his head, and Catherine could not move because of him—“because that boy there seems determined to defeat me, and I'd be obliged if his uncle would hurry up and go first! Hallo! Has the whelp been at that game long? I _did_ teach him a thing or two about snivelling. Is he usually fairly lively with Miss Linton?”
“Lively? No. He's been terribly distressed,” I answered. “Judging by his appearance, he ought to be in bed with a doctor attending him, instead of walking on the hills with his sweetheart.”
“He will be, in a day or two,” Heathcliff muttered. “But first—get up, Linton! Get up!” he shouted. “Stop grovelling on the ground. Up, this instant!”

Linton had collapsed again in another fit of helpless terror, brought on, I suppose, by his father's glance: nothing else could account for such abasement. He tried several times to obey, but for the moment his little strength had entirely deserted him, and he fell back with a groan. Mr. Heathcliff stepped forward and lifted him to lean against a ridge of turf.
“Now,” he said with barely restrained savagery, “I'm getting angry. And if you don't control that miserable spirit of yours—_damn_ you! Get up at once!”

“I will, father,” he panted. “Only leave me alone, or I'll faint. I'm sure I've done what you wanted. Catherine will tell you I've—that I've—been cheerful. Oh, stay beside me, Catherine! Give me your hand.”

“Take mine,” his father said. “Stand on your feet. There—she'll give you her arm. That's right, look at _her_. You'd think I was the devil himself, Miss Linton, to inspire such terror. Would you be so kind as to walk home with him? He shudders when I touch him.”
“Dear Linton,” Catherine whispered, “I can't go to Wuthering Heights. Papa has forbidden it. He won't hurt you. Why are you so frightened?”
“I can never go back into that house,” he answered. “I'm _not allowed_ to go back without you!”
“Enough!” his father cried. “We'll respect Catherine's scruples about obeying her father. Nelly, take him inside, and I'll follow your advice about a doctor at once.”
“That would be wise,” I replied. “But I must stay with my mistress. Looking after your son isn't my business.”

“You're very stubborn, I know,” said Heathcliff. “But you'll make me pinch the baby and set it screaming before I can stir your charity. Come along, then, my hero. Will you go home with me escorting you?”

He came towards him again as if to seize the frail creature. Linton shrank back and clung to his cousin, begging her to go with him with such frantic insistence that refusal was impossible. However much I disapproved, I could not stop her. Indeed, how could she herself have refused? We had no way of knowing what frightened him, but it held him helpless, and any further shock seemed enough to rob him of his wits. We reached the doorway. Catherine went in, and I waited while she helped the invalid to a chair, expecting her to return at once. Then Mr. Heathcliff pushed me forward, exclaiming, “My house hasn't got the plague, Nelly. And I'm feeling hospitable today. Sit down and let me shut the door.”
He not only shut it, but locked it. I started in alarm.

“You'll have tea before you go home,” he added. “I'm alone. Hareton has taken some cattle to the Lees, and Zillah and Joseph are away enjoying themselves. Though I'm used to solitude, I'd rather have interesting company when I can get it. Miss Linton, sit beside _him_. I give you what I've got. It's a present hardly worth accepting, but I have nothing else to offer. I mean Linton. How she stares! It's strange how savage I feel towards anything that seems frightened of me. If I'd been born somewhere with fewer laws and less delicate tastes, I'd amuse myself of an evening by slowly cutting those two open alive.”
He drew a breath, struck the table, and swore to himself, “By hell! I hate them.”

“I'm not afraid of you!” Catherine exclaimed. She had not heard the last part of his speech. She stepped right up to him, her dark eyes flashing with anger and determination. “Give me that key. I _will_ have it!” she said. “I wouldn't eat or drink in this house if I were starving.”

The key lay in Heathcliff's hand, which still rested on the table. He looked up, apparently surprised by her boldness—or perhaps her voice and look reminded him of the person from whom she had inherited it. She snatched at the key and almost pulled it from his slackened fingers. But her movement brought him back to the present, and he quickly recovered it.
“Now, Catherine Linton,” he said, “stand back, or I'll knock you down. And that will make Mrs. Dean furious.”

Ignoring the warning, she caught his closed hand and the key again. “We _will_ leave!” she repeated, struggling with all her strength to force those iron muscles to loosen. When her nails made no impression, she bit him sharply. Heathcliff shot me a look that stopped me intervening for a moment. Catherine was too intent on his fingers to notice his face. Suddenly he opened his hand and let her have the disputed object. But before she had a firm hold of it, he seized her with his freed hand and pulled her onto his knee. With the other hand he rained terrible blows on both sides of her head, any one of which would have fulfilled his threat if she had been free to fall.

At this fiendish violence I rushed at him in a fury. “You villain!” I began shouting. “You villain!” A push against my chest silenced me. I am stout and easily winded, and between that and my rage I staggered back dizzily, feeling as though I would suffocate or burst a blood vessel. It was all over in two minutes. Released, Catherine put both hands to her temples and looked as though she could not tell whether her ears were still attached. The poor girl shook like a reed and leaned against the table, utterly dazed.

“You see, I know how to discipline children,” the scoundrel said grimly, stooping to retrieve the key from the floor. “Now go to Linton as I told you, and cry as much as you please! Tomorrow I'll be your father—all the father you'll have in a few days—and you'll get plenty of that. You can take plenty; you're no weakling. You'll have a taste of it every day if I catch that devilish temper in your eyes again!”

Instead of going to Linton, Cathy ran to me, knelt down, and laid her burning cheek in my lap, sobbing aloud. Her cousin had shrunk into a corner of the settle, quiet as a mouse, no doubt congratulating himself that someone else had received the punishment. Seeing us all overwhelmed, Mr. Heathcliff stood up and briskly made the tea himself. The cups and saucers were already laid out. He poured the tea and handed me a cup.
“Wash down your anger,” he said. “And give some to your naughty pet and mine. It's not poisoned, though I made it. I'm going to find your horses.”
As soon as he left, our first thought was to force a way out. We tried the kitchen door, but it was fastened from outside. We examined the windows: they were too narrow even for Cathy's small figure.
“Master Linton,” I cried, realising we were truly imprisoned, “you know what that devil of a father of yours is planning, and you'll tell us, or I'll box your ears as he boxed your cousin's.”
“Yes, Linton, you must tell us,” Catherine said. “I came for your sake. Refusing would be wickedly ungrateful.”

“Give me some tea—I'm thirsty—and then I'll tell you,” he answered. “Mrs. Dean, move away. I don't like you standing over me. Now, Catherine, you're crying into my cup. I won't drink that. Give me another.”

Catherine pushed another cup towards him and wiped her face. The little wretch's calmness, now that he no longer feared for himself, disgusted me. His distress on the moor had vanished the moment he entered Wuthering Heights. I guessed he had been threatened with a terrible outburst of fury if he failed to lure us there, and now that he had succeeded he had nothing more to fear for the moment.

“Papa wants us to get married,” he continued after taking a sip. “He knows your papa wouldn't let us marry now, and he's afraid I'll die if we wait. So we're to marry tomorrow morning, and you must stay here all night. If you do what he wants, you can go home the day after and take me with you.”

“Take you with her, you pitiful changeling!” I exclaimed. “_You_, marry? The man's mad, or he thinks we're all fools. Do you imagine that beautiful young lady, that healthy, lively girl, will tie herself to a little dying monkey like you? Do you really believe _anyone_, let alone Miss Catherine Linton, would have you for a husband? You deserve a whipping for bringing us here at all with your cowardly, whining tricks. And don't look so stupid now! I've a very good mind to give you a thorough shaking for your contemptible treachery and your idiotic conceit.”
I did shake him a little, but it started his cough, and he fell back on his usual defence of groaning and crying. Catherine reproached me.
“Stay all night? No,” she said, slowly looking around. “Ellen, I'll burn that door down if that's what it takes to get out.”

She would have carried out her threat at once, but Linton sprang up, terrified for his precious self again. He clasped her in his two weak arms and sobbed, “Won't you marry me and save me? Won't you let me come to the Grange? Oh, darling Catherine, you mustn't leave me after all! You _must_ obey my father—you _must_!”

“I must obey my own,” she replied, “and put an end to this cruel uncertainty for him. The whole night! What would he think? He'll be worried already. I'll break my way out of this house or burn my way out. Be quiet! You're in no danger. But if you stop me—Linton, I love papa more than you!”

His mortal fear of Mr. Heathcliff's anger restored the boy's cowardly eloquence. Catherine was almost beside herself, but still insisted she must go home. Now she tried pleading too, urging him to master his selfish distress. While they were occupied in this way, our jailer came back.

“Your animals have trotted off,” he said. “And—now, Linton! Snivelling again? What's she been doing to you? Come, come, stop it and go to bed. In a month or two, my boy, you'll have a strong enough hand to repay her for bullying you now. You're wasting away from love alone, aren't you? Nothing else in the world. And she shall have you! Now, to bed. Zillah won't be here tonight; you'll have to undress yourself. Hush! Stop that noise! Once you're in your own room, I won't come near you. You needn't be frightened. You've managed tolerably well, by chance. I'll deal with the rest.”

As he spoke, he held the door open for his son. Linton slipped past exactly like a spaniel suspecting that the person attending to it meant to give it a spiteful squeeze. The door was locked again. Heathcliff came over to the fire, where my mistress and I stood silently. Catherine looked up and instinctively raised a hand to her cheek: his nearness had revived the pain. Anyone else would have been softened by that childish gesture, but he scowled at her and muttered, “Oh, so you're not afraid of me? You hide your courage well. You _seem_ damnably frightened!”

“I _am_ frightened now,” she replied, “because if I stay, papa will be miserable. And how can I bear to make him miserable when he—when he—Mr. Heathcliff, _let_ me go home! I promise I'll marry Linton. Papa would like me to, and I love him. Why force me to do something I'd willingly do myself?”

“Let him try to force you!” I cried. “Thank God there's law in this country, even in a place as remote as this! I'd report him if he were my own son. It's a felony, with no benefit of clergy to save him!”

“Silence!” the ruffian said. “To hell with your shouting! I don't want _you_ speaking. Miss Linton, the thought of your father's misery will give me immense pleasure. I shall be too satisfied to sleep. You couldn't have found a surer way of keeping yourself under my roof for the next twenty-four hours than telling me that would be the result. As for your promise to marry Linton, I'll see that you keep it. You won't leave here until you have.”
“Then send Ellen to tell papa I'm safe!” Catherine cried, weeping bitterly. “Or marry me now. Poor papa! Ellen, he'll think we're lost. What can we do?”

“Nothing of the sort! He'll think you've grown tired of nursing him and run off for a little amusement,” Heathcliff answered. “You can't deny you came into my house of your own accord, against his express orders. And it's quite natural to want amusement at your age, and to grow tired of nursing a sick man when he's _only_ your father. Catherine, his happiest days ended when your life began. I dare say he cursed you for coming into the world—I certainly did—and it would be only fitting if he cursed you as _he_ left it. I'd join him. I don't love you! Why should I? Cry away. From what I can see, crying will be your chief amusement from now on, unless Linton makes up for your other losses. Your far-seeing parent seems to think he might. His letters of advice and comfort entertained me enormously. In the last one he told my jewel to take care of his, and to be kind to her once he had her. Careful and kind—how fatherly! But Linton needs all his care and kindness for himself. He makes an excellent little tyrant. He'll torture any number of cats, provided their teeth have been pulled and their claws cut. You'll have fine stories of his _kindness_ for his uncle when you get home, I assure you.”
“Quite right!” I said. “Explain your son's character. Show her how like you he is. Then I hope Miss Cathy will think twice before she takes that cockatrice!”

“I don't much mind discussing his charming qualities now,” he answered. “She must either accept him or stay a prisoner, with you beside her, until your master dies. I can keep you both here completely hidden. If you doubt it, encourage her to break her promise. Then you'll have a chance to find out!”

“I won't break my promise,” Catherine said. “I'll marry him within the hour if I can go to Thrushcross Grange afterwards. Mr. Heathcliff, you're cruel, but you're not a fiend. You won't destroy all my happiness for ever out of _pure_ malice. If papa thought I'd left him deliberately, and died before I got back, how could I bear to live? I've stopped crying. But I'm going to kneel here beside your knee, and I won't get up or take my eyes off your face until you look back at me! No, don't turn away. _Do_ look! You won't see anything to anger you. I don't hate you. I'm not angry that you hit me. Have you never loved _anyone_ in your whole life, uncle? _Never_? Ah, you must look at me once. I'm so miserable, you can't help feeling sorry for me and pitying me.”

“Keep your lizard fingers off me! Move, or I'll kick you!” Heathcliff cried, roughly thrusting her away. “I'd rather be embraced by a snake. How the devil can you think of fawning on me? I _detest_ you!”

He shrugged, then actually shook himself as though disgust made his flesh crawl, and pushed back his chair. I stood up and opened my mouth to unleash a torrent of abuse. But he silenced me halfway through my first sentence by threatening to put me in a room alone if I uttered another syllable. It was getting dark. We heard voices at the garden gate. Our host hurried out at once. _He_ had kept his wits; _we_ had not. After two or three minutes of conversation, he came back alone.
“I thought that was your cousin Hareton,” I said to Catherine. “I wish he'd come! Who knows—he might take our side.”

“It was three servants from the Grange, sent to look for you,” Heathcliff said, overhearing me. “You should have opened a window and called out. But I'd swear the little minx is glad you didn't. I'm certain she's pleased to be forced to stay.”

When we learnt what chance we had missed, we both gave way to uncontrollable grief. He let us cry until nine, then ordered us upstairs through the kitchen to Zillah's room. I whispered to my companion to obey: perhaps we could get through the window there, or into an attic and out through its skylight. But the window was as narrow as those downstairs, and the attic trapdoor was beyond our reach, for we were locked in as before. Neither of us lay down. Catherine stood by the window, anxiously watching for morning. My repeated pleas that she try to rest brought only a deep sigh. I sat in a chair rocking backwards and forwards, bitterly condemning the many times I had failed in my duty. It seemed to me then that all my employers' misfortunes had sprung from those failures. I know that was not really true, but on that wretched night I imagined it was, and thought even Heathcliff less guilty than myself.

At seven he came and asked whether Miss Linton was up. She ran straight to the door and answered yes. “Come, then,” he said, opening it and pulling her out. I got up to follow, but he locked it again. I demanded to be let out.
“Be patient,” he replied. “I'll send your breakfast up in a little while.”

I hammered on the panels and angrily rattled the latch. Catherine asked why I was still locked in. He said I must try to bear it for another hour, and they went away. I bore it for two or three hours. At last I heard footsteps, which were not Heathcliff's.
“I've brought ye something to eat,” a voice said. “Open t' door!”
I hurried to obey and found Hareton carrying enough food to last me the day.
“Take it,” he added, thrusting the tray into my hands.
“Wait a moment,” I began.
“Nay,” he cried, and left, paying no attention to any plea I could make to hold him there.

I remained locked up all that day, all the following night, and then another, and another. Altogether I spent five nights and four days there, seeing nobody but Hareton once each morning. He was a perfect jailer: surly and silent, deaf to every attempt to appeal to his justice or compassion.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVIII
paragraphs: On the fifth morning—or rather, afternoon—I heard a different step approaching, lighter and shorter. This time the visitor came into the room. It was Zillah, wearing her scarlet shawl and a black silk bonnet, with a wicker basket on her arm.

“Dear me, Mrs. Dean!” she exclaimed. “Well, they're talking about you in Gimmerton! I thought you'd sunk in the Blackhorse marsh, with missy beside you, until the master told me you'd been found and he was keeping you here! You must have got onto an island, surely? How long were you stuck in that hole? Did the master save you, Mrs. Dean? But you haven't grown so thin. You haven't been that poorly, have you?”
“Your master is a thorough scoundrel!” I answered. “But he'll answer for it. He needn't have made up that story. I'll expose the whole thing!”

“What do you mean?” Zillah asked. “It's not his story. That's what they're saying in the village—that you were lost in the marsh. When I came in, I called to Earnshaw, ‘Eh, Mr. Hareton, strange things have happened while I've been away. What a pity about that fine young girl and lively Nelly Dean.’ He stared. I thought he hadn't heard, so I told him the rumour. The master listened, then just smiled to himself and said, ‘If they've been in the marsh, they're out now, Zillah. Nelly Dean is staying in your room this very minute. When you go up, tell her to be off. Here's the key. The bog water went to her head, and she'd have run home quite delirious, but I kept her here until she came to her senses. Tell her to go to the Grange at once if she's able, and take a message from me: her young lady will follow in time for the squire's funeral.’”
“Mr. Edgar isn't dead?” I gasped. “Oh, Zillah, Zillah!”
“No, no. Sit down, my good woman,” she replied. “You're still quite unwell. He's not dead. Doctor Kenneth thinks he might last another day. I met him on the road and asked.”

Instead of sitting down, I snatched up my outdoor clothes and hurried downstairs, since the way was open. In the main room I looked for someone who could tell me about Catherine. Sunlight filled the room, and the door stood wide open, but no one seemed to be there. I hesitated between leaving at once and going back to look for my mistress. Then a faint cough drew my attention to the hearth. Linton was lying alone on the settle, sucking a stick of sugar candy and following my movements with indifferent eyes. “Where is Miss Catherine?” I demanded sternly, thinking that, now I had caught him alone, I could frighten him into answering. He went on sucking his sweet as innocently as ever.
“Has she gone?” I asked.
“No,” he answered. “She's upstairs. She's not allowed to go. We won't let her.”
“You won't let her, you little idiot!” I exclaimed. “Tell me where her room is this minute, or I'll make you cry out.”

“Papa would make _you_ cry out if you tried to go there,” he replied. “He says I mustn't be soft with Catherine. She's my wife, and it's disgraceful of her to want to leave me. He says she hates me and wants me to die so she can have my money. But she shan't have it, and she shan't go home! Never! She can cry and be ill as much as she likes!”
He went back to his sweet, closing his eyes as though he intended to fall asleep.

“Master Heathcliff,” I began again, “have you forgotten all Catherine's kindness last winter, when you said you loved her? She brought you books and sang to you, and came again and again through wind and snow to see you. She cried if she missed one evening because you'd be disappointed. You felt then that she was a hundred times too good to you. And now you believe your father's lies, though you know he hates you both. You take his side against her. What fine gratitude!”
The corner of Linton's mouth drooped, and he took the sugar candy away from his lips.

“Did she come to Wuthering Heights because she hated you?” I went on. “Think for yourself! As for your money, she doesn't even know you'll have any. You say she's ill, yet you leave her alone upstairs in a strange house! _You_, who know what it means to be neglected like that! You could pity your own suffering, and she pitied it too, but you won't pity hers. Look, Master Heathcliff, I'm crying—an older woman, and only a servant. Yet you, after pretending to love her so much, and with almost every reason to worship her, save all your tears for yourself and lie there quite comfortably. Oh, you're a heartless, selfish boy!”

“I can't stay with her,” he answered crossly. “And I won't stay on my own. She cries so much I can't bear it. She won't stop even when I tell her I'll call my father. I did call him once, and he threatened to strangle her if she wasn't quiet. But the moment he left she started again, groaning and grieving all night, though I screamed with annoyance because I couldn't sleep.”
“Is Mr. Heathcliff out?” I asked, seeing that the miserable creature was incapable of feeling for his cousin's mental agony.

“He's in the yard,” he replied, “talking to Doctor Kenneth, who says uncle really is dying at last. I'm glad: I'll be master of the Grange after him. Catherine always called it _her_ house. It isn't hers! It's mine. Papa says everything she has belongs to me. All her lovely books are mine. She offered them to me, and her pretty birds and her pony Minny, if I'd get our room key and let her out. But I told her she had nothing to give: it was all, all mine. Then she cried and took a little picture from around her neck and said I could have that. There were two pictures in a gold case, her mother on one side and uncle on the other, when they were young. That was yesterday. I said _those_ were mine too, and tried to take them. The spiteful thing wouldn't let me. She pushed me away and hurt me. I screamed—that frightens her. She heard papa coming, broke the hinges to separate the case, and gave me her mother's picture. She tried to hide the other one, but papa asked what was wrong, and I told him. He took my picture away and ordered her to give me hers. She refused, and he—he knocked her down, tore it off the chain, and crushed it under his foot.”
“Did it please you to see her hit?” I asked. I had a purpose in encouraging him to talk.

“I flinched,” he answered. “I flinch when my father hits a dog or a horse, he hits so hard. But I was glad at first. She deserved punishment for pushing me. After papa went, though, she made me come to the window and showed me where her teeth had cut the inside of her cheek and how her mouth was filling with blood. Then she picked up the pieces of the picture and sat down facing the wall. She hasn't spoken to me since. Sometimes I think she's in too much pain to speak. I don't like thinking that, but she's naughty to keep crying. And she looks so pale and wild that I'm afraid of her.”
“So you can get the key if you want to?” I said.
“Yes, when I'm upstairs,” he answered. “But I can't walk up there now.”
“Which room is it in?” I asked.

“Oh, I'm not telling _you_ where it is!” he cried. “That's our secret. Nobody's to know, not Hareton or Zillah. There, you've tired me out. Go away, go away!” He turned his face onto his arm and closed his eyes again.

I decided it would be best to leave without seeing Mr. Heathcliff and bring help from the Grange to rescue my young mistress. When I arrived there, my fellow servants were overwhelmed with surprise and joy. On hearing that their little mistress was safe, two or three were ready to rush upstairs and shout the news through Mr. Edgar's door, but I insisted on telling him myself. How much he had changed, even in those few days! He lay awaiting death, the picture of sadness and resignation. He looked very young. He was thirty-nine, but anyone would have taken him for at least ten years younger. His thoughts were on Catherine, for he murmured her name. I touched his hand and spoke.
“Catherine is coming, dear master,” I whispered. “She's alive and well. I hope she'll be here tonight.”

His first response to the news frightened me. He half sat up, looked eagerly around the room, then sank back unconscious. Once he recovered, I told him about our forced visit and imprisonment at the Heights. I said Heathcliff had made me go inside, which was not quite true. I spoke as little as possible against Linton and did not describe all his father's brutality. If I could help it, I meant to add no further bitterness to a cup already overflowing.

He understood that one of his enemy's aims was to secure the personal fortune as well as the estate for his son—or rather, for himself. But my master could not understand why he had not waited for his death, being unaware how close together he and his nephew would leave the world. Still, he thought it best to change his will. Instead of leaving Catherine free to dispose of her fortune, he decided to place it in the hands of trustees for her use during her lifetime, and afterwards for any children she might have. That way it could not pass to Mr. Heathcliff if Linton died.

On his orders, I sent one man for the lawyer and four others, equipped with useful weapons, to demand my young mistress from her jailer. Both parties were delayed until very late. The servant sent alone returned first. Mr. Green, the lawyer, had been out, he said, and he had waited two hours for him. Then Mr. Green said he had a little business in the village that must be attended to, but would be at Thrushcross Grange before morning. The other four men also returned without her. Catherine was ill, they reported, too ill to leave her room, and Heathcliff would not let them see her. I gave the fools a thorough scolding for believing that tale and refused to repeat it to my master. At daylight, I resolved, I would take a whole crowd to the Heights and literally storm the house unless they handed over their prisoner peacefully. Her father _would_ see her, I swore again and again, even if that devil had to be killed on his own doorstep for trying to stop it!

Fortunately, I was spared both the journey and the struggle. At three o'clock I had gone downstairs for a jug of water and was carrying it through the hall when a sharp knock at the front door startled me. “Oh, it's Green,” I said, recovering myself. “Only Green.” I walked on, meaning to send someone else to let him in, but the knock came again, not loudly, yet insistently. I set the jug on the banister and hurried to the door myself. Outside, the harvest moon shone clearly. It was not the lawyer. My own dear little mistress flung her arms around my neck, sobbing, “Ellen, Ellen! Is papa alive?”
“Yes!” I cried. “Yes, my angel, he is! Thank God you're safely back with us!”

Breathless as she was, she wanted to run upstairs to Mr. Linton's room. I made her sit down instead, gave her something to drink, and washed her pale face, rubbing it with my apron until a little colour returned. Then I told her I must go first to announce her arrival. I begged her to say she would be happy with young Heathcliff. She stared at me, but soon understood why I was urging her to tell that lie, and promised she would not complain.

I couldn't bear to witness their reunion. For a quarter of an hour I stood outside the bedroom door, and even then hardly dared approach the bed. But all was quiet. Catherine's despair was as silent as her father's joy. To outward appearances she supported him calmly, while he raised his eyes to her face, and they seemed to widen with rapture.

He died in perfect happiness, Mr. Lockwood. That is how he died. Kissing her cheek, he murmured, “I'm going to her, and you, darling child, will come to us!” He never moved or spoke again, but kept that radiant, absorbed gaze until his pulse stopped imperceptibly and his soul left him. No one could have marked the exact moment of his death. There was no struggle at all.

Whether Catherine had no tears left, or her grief was too heavy to let them flow, she sat there dry-eyed until sunrise. She stayed until noon and would have gone on keeping watch over that deathbed if I had not insisted she come away and rest. It was fortunate I persuaded her, for at dinner time the lawyer arrived, having first called at Wuthering Heights for instructions. He had sold himself to Mr. Heathcliff: that explained his delay in answering my master's summons. Fortunately, after his daughter's return, no thoughts of worldly business had troubled the dying man's mind.

Mr. Green assumed authority over everyone and everything in the house. He dismissed all the servants except me. He would even have stretched his borrowed powers so far as to insist that Edgar Linton be buried in the chapel with his family rather than beside his wife. But the will prevented that, along with my loud protests against any departure from its instructions. The funeral was hurried through. Catherine, now Mrs. Linton Heathcliff, was allowed to remain at the Grange until her father's body had been taken away.

She told me that her agony had finally driven Linton to risk setting her free. She had heard my men arguing at the door and understood the meaning of Heathcliff's answer. It made her desperate. Linton, who had been carried up to the little parlour soon after I left, was frightened into fetching the key before his father came upstairs again. He was cunning enough to unlock the door and turn the lock again without shutting it. When bedtime came, he asked to sleep with Hareton, and for once his request was granted. Catherine slipped out before dawn. Afraid the dogs would raise the alarm, she dared not try the doors. Instead she searched the empty rooms and examined their windows. Luckily she found her mother's room, and by the fir tree close beside it she easily climbed out of the window and down to the ground. Despite his timid precautions, her accomplice suffered for his part in the escape.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIX
paragraphs: The evening after the funeral, my young mistress and I sat in the library, sometimes dwelling sorrowfully—one of us hopelessly—on our loss, sometimes daring to speculate about the dark future ahead.

We had just agreed that the best Catherine could hope for was permission to stay at the Grange, at least while Linton lived, with him allowed to join her and me to remain as housekeeper. It seemed almost too favourable an arrangement to hope for. Yet I did hope, and began to take comfort in the prospect of keeping my home and work, and above all my beloved young mistress. Just then a servant, one of those dismissed but not yet gone, rushed in to say “that devil Heathcliff” was crossing the yard. Should he shut the door in his face?

Even if we had been mad enough to order that, there was no time. He did not trouble to knock or announce himself. He was the master and used the master's privilege of walking straight in without a word. The servant's voice led him to the library. He entered, motioned the man out, and shut the door.

It was the same room into which he had been shown as a guest eighteen years earlier. The same moon shone through the window, and the same autumn landscape lay outside. We had not yet lit a candle, but the whole room was visible, including the portraits on the wall: Mrs. Linton's magnificent head and her husband's graceful one. Heathcliff walked towards the hearth. Time had changed his appearance very little either. He was the same man, his dark face a little more sallow and composed, his body perhaps a stone or two heavier, but otherwise unchanged. At the sight of him, Catherine had jumped up, meaning to rush out.

“Stop!” he said, catching her arm. “No more running away! Where would you go? I've come to take you home. I hope you'll be a dutiful daughter and won't encourage my son to disobey me again. When I discovered his part in the affair, I hardly knew how to punish him. He's such a cobweb that a pinch would destroy him. But you'll see from his face that he's had his due! The evening before last I brought him downstairs and put him in a chair, and didn't touch him afterwards. I sent Hareton out, so we had the room to ourselves. Two hours later I called Joseph to carry him upstairs again. Since then my presence has affected his nerves as powerfully as a ghost, and I fancy he often sees me when I'm nowhere near. Hareton says he wakes and screams for hours in the night, calling for you to protect him from me. Whether you like your precious husband or not, you must come. He's your responsibility now. I hand over all my concern in him to you.”
“Why not let Catherine stay here,” I pleaded, “and send Master Linton to her? Since you hate them both, you wouldn't miss them. They _must_ be a daily nuisance to that unnatural heart of yours.”

“I'm looking for a tenant for the Grange,” he answered, “and of course I want my children around me. Besides, the girl owes me work for her keep. I'm not going to support her in idleness and luxury after Linton's gone. Hurry up and get ready, now. Don't make me force you.”

“I will,” Catherine said. “Linton is all I have left in the world to love. You've done everything you could to make me hate him and him hate me, but you _can't_ make us hate each other. And I defy you to hurt him while I'm there. I defy you to frighten me!”

“What a boastful defender you are,” Heathcliff replied. “But I don't like you enough to hurt him. You'll have the full benefit of that torment for as long as it lasts. I won't be the one who makes you hate him: his own sweet nature will do that. He's bitter as gall about your desertion and its consequences. Don't expect thanks for this noble devotion. I heard him painting Zillah a pretty picture of what he'd do if he were as strong as me. The will is there, and his very weakness will sharpen his wits to find something to replace strength.”

“I know his nature is bad,” Catherine said. “He's your son. But I'm glad mine is better, so I can forgive it. I know he loves me, and that's why I love him. Mr. Heathcliff, _you_ have _no one_ who loves you. However miserable you make us, we'll still have the revenge of knowing your cruelty comes from being even more miserable yourself. You _are_ miserable, aren't you? Lonely as the devil, and envious like him? _Nobody_ loves you. _Nobody_ will cry when you die! I wouldn't be you!”
She spoke with a bleak sort of triumph. It seemed she had resolved to adopt the spirit of the family she was joining and find pleasure in her enemies' suffering.
“You'll soon be sorry to be yourself,” her father-in-law said, “if you stand there a minute longer. Off with you, witch! Get your things!”

She left with a look of contempt. While she was gone, I began begging to take Zillah's place at the Heights, offering to give up mine to her. He would not hear of it. He ordered me to be quiet, then for the first time let his eyes travel around the room and over the portraits. After studying Mrs. Linton's, he said, “I'll have that taken home. Not that I need it, but—” He turned sharply towards the fire and continued with what, for want of a better word, I must call a smile. “I'll tell you what I did yesterday. The sexton was digging Linton's grave. I got him to clear the earth from her coffin lid, and I opened it. For a moment I thought I'd stay there. When I saw her face again—it's still her face!—he could hardly move me. But he said it would change if the air reached it, so I loosened one side of the coffin and covered it up. Not the side nearest Linton, damn him! I wish he'd been sealed in lead. I bribed the sexton to pull that side away when I'm buried there and slide mine out too—I'll have my coffin made that way.
