Then by the time Linton reaches us, he won't know which is which!”
“That was very wicked, Mr. Heathcliff!” I exclaimed. “Weren't you ashamed to disturb the dead?”

“I disturbed no one, Nelly,” he replied, “and I brought myself some peace. I'll be much more comfortable now, and you'll have a better chance of keeping me underground once I'm there. Disturb her? No! She's disturbed me, day and night, for eighteen years—without rest, without mercy—until last night. Last night I was at peace. I dreamt I was sleeping my last sleep beside her, my heart stopped and my cheek frozen against hers.”
“And if she'd crumbled into earth, or something worse, what would you have dreamt then?” I asked.

“Of crumbling with her, and being happier still!” he answered. “Do you think I fear any change like that? I expected it when I lifted the lid, but I'm better pleased that it should wait until I can share it. Besides, without that clear impression of her still, untroubled features, I could hardly have shaken off that strange feeling. It began in an odd way. You know how wild I was after her death, praying without end, from dawn to dawn, for her spirit to return to me! I believe strongly in ghosts. I'm convinced they can exist among us, and do! Snow fell on the day she was buried. That evening I went to the churchyard. The wind was bleak as winter, and the place was deserted. I wasn't afraid her fool of a husband would wander up the valley so late, and no one else had any reason to be there. Alone, knowing that only two yards of loose earth stood between us, I said to myself, ‘I'll hold her in my arms again! If she's cold, I'll think it's this north wind chilling _me_. If she doesn't move, she's asleep.’ I fetched a spade from the tool shed and dug with all my strength. It scraped the coffin. I began working with my hands, and the wood started cracking around the screws. I was just about to succeed when I seemed to hear someone sigh above me, bending down close to the edge of the grave. ‘If only I can get this off,’ I muttered, ‘let them shovel the earth over both of us!’ I wrenched at it more desperately than ever. Another sigh came close to my ear. I seemed to feel its warm breath push aside the sleet-filled wind. I knew no living person of flesh and blood was there. But as surely as you sense yourself approaching a solid object in the dark without being able to see it, I felt Cathy there—not beneath me, but above ground. Relief suddenly flowed from my heart through every limb. I abandoned that agonising labour and turned away, instantly comforted—comforted beyond words. Her presence stayed with me while I filled in the grave, and led me home. Laugh if you like, but I was certain I'd see her there. I knew she was with me and couldn't help speaking to her. When I reached the Heights, I rushed eagerly to the door. It was locked. I remember that accursed Earnshaw and my wife trying to keep me out. I remember stopping to kick the breath out of him, then hurrying upstairs to the room that had been mine and hers. I looked impatiently around. I felt her beside me. I could _almost_ see her, and yet I _could not_! I should have sweated blood then from the agony of longing, from the desperate force of my prayers for just one glimpse. I got none. She proved herself a devil to me, as she so often had in life! Since then, more at some times and less at others, I've been the plaything of that unbearable torture. Hellish! It has kept my nerves stretched so tight that, if they hadn't been made of catgut, they would long ago have gone as slack and feeble as Linton's. Sitting in the house with Hareton, I'd feel that if I went out I'd meet her. Walking on the moors, I'd feel I'd meet her when I came in. Whenever I left home I hurried back. She _must_ be somewhere at the Heights; I was certain of it! As for sleeping in her room—I was driven out of that. I couldn't lie there. The moment I closed my eyes she was outside the window, or pushing back the panels, or coming through the door, or even resting her darling head on the same pillow as she used to as a child. I had to open my eyes and look. So I opened and closed them a hundred times a night, always to be disappointed! It tortured me! I've often groaned aloud until that old scoundrel Joseph must have thought my conscience was playing the devil inside me. Now that I've seen her, I'm calmer—a little. What a strange way to kill a man: not by inches, but by fractions of a hair's breadth, luring me on with the ghost of a hope for eighteen years!”

Mr. Heathcliff stopped and wiped his forehead, where his hair clung wet with sweat. His eyes were fixed on the red embers. His eyebrows were not drawn together but raised towards the temples, making his face less grim, yet giving it a peculiar troubled look, a painful appearance of a mind strained towards one all-consuming subject. He was only half speaking to me, and I kept quiet. I did not like hearing him talk! After a short while he returned his attention to the portrait, took it down, and leaned it against the sofa to see it better. While he was occupied with it, Catherine came in and announced that she was ready as soon as her pony was saddled.

“Send that over tomorrow,” Heathcliff told me. Then he turned to her. “You can do without the pony. It's a fine evening, and you won't need ponies at Wuthering Heights. Your own feet will do for any journeys you make. Come along.”
“Goodbye, Ellen,” my dear little mistress whispered. Her lips were icy as she kissed me. “Come and see me, Ellen. Don't forget.”
“Make sure you do nothing of the sort, Mrs. Dean!” said her new father. “When I want to speak to you, I'll come here. I don't want you prying around my house!”

He motioned her ahead of him. With a backward look that cut me to the heart, she obeyed. From the window I watched them go down the garden. Heathcliff tucked Catherine's arm under his, though she clearly resisted at first, and hurried her with long strides into the avenue, where the trees hid them from sight.

chapters.title: Chapter XXX
paragraphs: I have been to the Heights, but I have not seen her since she left. When I called to ask about her, Joseph held the door and would not let me in. He said Mrs. Linton was “busy” and the master was out. Zillah has told me something of their life there; otherwise I would scarcely know who was alive and who was dead. From the way she talks, I gather that she thinks Catherine proud and dislikes her. When my young mistress first arrived, she asked Zillah for help, but Mr. Heathcliff told the woman to mind her own business and let his daughter-in-law look after herself. Zillah, being narrow-minded and selfish, was quite willing to obey. Catherine resented this neglect like a child and answered it with contempt, making an enemy of my informant as surely as if she had done her some terrible injury. About six weeks ago, shortly before you came, I met Zillah on the moor and had a long talk with her. This is what she told me.

“The first thing Mrs. Linton did when she reached the Heights,” she said, “was run upstairs without even saying good evening to me or Joseph. She shut herself in Linton's room and stayed there until morning. Then, while the master and Earnshaw were having breakfast, she came down into the main room, trembling all over, and asked if we could send for the doctor. Her cousin was very ill.
“‘We know that!’ Heathcliff answered. ‘But his life isn't worth a farthing, and I won't spend a farthing on him.’
“‘But I don't know what to do,’ she said. ‘If nobody helps me, he'll die!’
“‘Get out of this room,’ the master cried, ‘and don't let me hear another word about him! Nobody here cares what happens to him. If you care, nurse him. If you don't, lock him up and leave him.’

“Then she started bothering me. I told her I'd had enough trouble with the tiresome creature. We each had our work, and hers was to look after Linton. Mr. Heathcliff had told me to leave that job to her.

“I can't say how they managed together. I imagine he fretted a great deal and lay groaning day and night, and she got precious little rest. You could tell from her white face and heavy eyes. Sometimes she came into the kitchen looking quite bewildered, as though she wanted to beg for help. But I wasn't going to disobey the master. I never dare disobey him, Mrs. Dean. Though I thought it wrong not to send for Kenneth, it wasn't my place to advise or complain, and I always refused to interfere. Once or twice, after we'd gone to bed, I happened to open my door and see her sitting at the top of the stairs crying. Then I shut myself in quickly, for fear I'd be moved to do something. I did feel sorry for her then, certainly. Still, I didn't want to lose my position, you understand.
“At last, one night she walked straight into my room and frightened me out of my wits by saying, ‘Tell Mr. Heathcliff his son is dying. I'm certain of it this time. Get up at once and tell him.’
“Then she disappeared again. I lay there listening and trembling for a quarter of an hour. Nothing moved. The house was silent.

“She's mistaken, I told myself. He's recovered. There's no need to disturb them. I began to doze, but a sharp ringing of the bell woke me again—the only bell we have, installed specially for Linton. The master called to me to find out what was wrong and tell them he wouldn't have that noise again.

“I gave him Catherine's message. He swore to himself, and a few minutes later came out with a lighted candle and went to their room. I followed him. Mrs. Heathcliff sat beside the bed with her hands folded on her knees. Her father-in-law approached, held the candle to Linton's face, looked at him and touched him, then turned to her.
“‘Well, Catherine,’ he said, ‘how do you feel?’
“She said nothing.
“‘How do you feel, Catherine?’ he asked again.

“‘He's safe, and I'm free,’ she answered. ‘I ought to feel well. But’—she couldn't hide her bitterness—‘you've left me struggling alone against death so long that death is all I can see or feel! I feel like death!’

“And she looked like it! I gave her a little wine. Hareton and Joseph had been woken by the bell and footsteps and had heard us talking from outside; now they came in. I think Joseph was pleased to be rid of the boy. Hareton looked a little troubled, though he was more occupied with staring at Catherine than thinking about Linton. The master told him to go back to bed: we didn't need his help. Afterwards he made Joseph carry the body to his own room and told me to go back to mine, leaving Mrs. Heathcliff alone.

“In the morning he sent me to tell her to come down for breakfast. She'd undressed and seemed about to sleep. She said she was ill, which hardly surprised me. I told Mr. Heathcliff, and he said, ‘Well, leave her alone until after the funeral. Go up now and then and bring her what she needs. Tell me as soon as she seems better.’”

According to Zillah, Cathy stayed upstairs for a fortnight. Zillah visited twice a day and would have been somewhat friendlier, but every attempt at greater kindness was immediately and proudly rejected.

Heathcliff went up once to show her Linton's will. He had left his father all his own movable property and everything of that kind which had formerly been hers. The poor creature had been threatened or coaxed into doing it during the week she was away, when his uncle died. Being under age, he could not dispose of the land. Yet Mr. Heathcliff has claimed and kept it through his wife's rights and his own—legally, I suppose. At any rate Catherine, with no money and no friends, cannot challenge his possession.

“Except for that one time,” Zillah said, “I was the only person who ever came to her door, and nobody asked about her. She first came down into the main room on a Sunday afternoon. When I took up her dinner, she'd cried out that she couldn't bear the cold any longer. I told her the master was going to Thrushcross Grange, and Earnshaw and I needn't stop her coming downstairs. So as soon as she heard Heathcliff's horse trot away, she appeared. She was dressed in black, with her yellow curls combed back behind her ears as plainly as a Quaker's. She couldn't comb the curl out of them.

“Joseph and I generally go to chapel on Sundays”—the church has no minister now, Mrs. Dean explained; they call the Methodist or Baptist place in Gimmerton a chapel, I couldn't tell you which it is—“and Joseph had gone,” she continued, “but I thought it best to stay at home. Young people are always better with an older person watching them, and for all his shyness, Hareton isn't a model of good manners. I told him his cousin would probably sit with us, and that she was used to seeing the Sabbath respected. He'd better leave his guns and indoor jobs alone while she was there. He went red at the news and looked down at his hands and clothes. The whale oil and gunpowder disappeared in a moment. I saw he meant to keep her company, and guessed from his manner that he wanted to look presentable. So I laughed, as I wouldn't dare with the master there, offered to help him if he liked, and teased him about his embarrassment. He turned sulky and began swearing.

“Now, Mrs. Dean,” Zillah went on, seeing that her manner displeased me, “perhaps you think your young lady too fine for Mr. Hareton. Perhaps you're right. But I admit I'd be glad to see her pride brought down a peg. What good will all her learning and fine ways do her now? She's as poor as you or me—poorer, I'll wager. You're saving, and I'm doing my little bit that way too.”

Hareton let Zillah help him, and her flattery put him in a good humour. So when Catherine appeared, he partly forgot her earlier insults and tried, according to the housekeeper, to make himself agreeable.

“The mistress walked in,” she said, “cold as an icicle and proud as a princess. I stood up and offered her my armchair. No—she turned up her nose at my kindness. Earnshaw stood too and invited her to sit on the settle close to the fire. He said she must be frozen.
“‘I've been frozen for a month and more,’ she answered, putting all the contempt she could into the word.

“She fetched her own chair and set it away from both of us. After she'd sat long enough to warm up, she looked around and noticed some books on the dresser. At once she stood and reached for them, but they were too high. Her cousin watched her trying for a while, then at last found the courage to help. She held out her skirt, and he filled it with the first books he could reach.

“That was a great step forward for the lad. She didn't thank him, but he was pleased that she'd accepted his help. He ventured to stand behind her while she looked through them, even bending down to point out things he liked in some of the old pictures. The rude way she jerked the page away from his finger didn't discourage him. He merely moved back a little and looked at her instead of the book. She went on reading, or looking for something to read. Gradually all his attention settled on her thick, silky curls. He couldn't see her face, and she couldn't see him. Perhaps without quite knowing what he was doing, drawn like a child to a candle, he finally went from looking to touching. He reached out and stroked one curl as gently as if it were a bird. You'd have thought he'd stuck a knife in her neck, the way she spun around in a fury.
“‘Go away this instant! How dare you touch me? Why are you standing there?’ she cried in disgust. ‘I can't bear you! If you come near me, I'll go upstairs again.’

“Mr. Hareton drew back, looking as foolish as could be, and sat very quietly on the settle. She went on turning through her books for another half-hour. At last Earnshaw came over and whispered to me.
“‘Will ye ask her to read to us, Zillah? I'm tired of doing nowt, and I do like—I would like to hear her! Don't say I asked. Ask her for thysen.’
“‘Mr. Hareton would like you to read to us, ma'am,’ I said at once. ‘He'd think it very kind. He'd be much obliged.’
“She frowned, looked up, and answered—

“‘Mr. Hareton, and all the rest of you, will kindly understand that I reject every sham kindness you're hypocritical enough to offer! I despise you and want nothing to do with any of you! When I'd have given my life for one kind word, even the sight of one of your faces, you all stayed away. But I won't complain to you. The cold has driven me down here. I haven't come to entertain you or enjoy your company.’
“‘What could I have done?’ Earnshaw began. ‘How was I to blame?’
“‘Oh, you're an exception,’ Mrs. Heathcliff replied. ‘I never missed anything like you.’
“‘But I offered more than once, and I asked,’ he said, growing angry at her insolence. ‘I asked Mr. Heathcliff to let me sit up for you—’
“‘Be quiet! I'll go outside, or anywhere at all, rather than listen to that horrible voice of yours!’ my lady said.

“Hareton muttered that she could go to hell for all he cared. He took down his gun and no longer held back from his Sunday occupations. He talked freely enough now, and before long she chose to retreat to her solitude. But the frost had arrived, and despite her pride she had to stoop to joining us more and more often. I made sure she had no further chance to sneer at my kindness. Ever since then I've been as cold as she is. Nobody here loves her or likes her, and she doesn't deserve it. Let anyone say the least thing to her and she bristles, with no respect for anyone. She'll snap even at the master, almost daring him to beat her, and the more she's hurt, the more spiteful she becomes.”

When Zillah first told me this, I resolved to leave my position, take a cottage, and persuade Catherine to live with me. But Mr. Heathcliff would no more allow that than he would set Hareton up in a house of his own. At present I can see no way out unless she marries again, and that is not something I have the power to arrange.

So Mrs. Dean's story ended. Despite the doctor's prediction, I am rapidly regaining my strength. Though it is only the second week of January, I mean to get out on horseback in a day or two and ride to Wuthering Heights. I shall tell my landlord that I intend to spend the next six months in London, and that he may, if he wishes, find another tenant to take the house after October. Nothing short of a great reward would make me spend another winter here.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXI
paragraphs: Yesterday was clear, still, and frosty. I went to the Heights as planned. My housekeeper begged me to carry a short note to her young mistress, and I agreed, since the good woman saw nothing odd in the request. The front door stood open, but the unwelcoming gate was locked, as on my previous visit. I knocked, calling Earnshaw away from the garden beds. He unfastened the chain and let me in. The fellow is as handsome a countryman as one could wish to see. I noticed him particularly this time, though he seems determined to make as little as possible of his advantages.

I asked whether Mr. Heathcliff was home. He said no, but he would return for dinner. It was eleven o'clock. When I said I would go in and wait, he immediately put down his tools and came with me, acting as a watchdog rather than a substitute host.

We went in together. Catherine was there, making herself useful by preparing vegetables for the coming meal. She looked sulkier and less spirited than when I first saw her. She barely raised her eyes at my arrival and continued her task with the same disregard for ordinary politeness as before, offering not the slightest acknowledgment of my bow or good morning.
“She doesn't seem as pleasant as Mrs. Dean would have me believe,” I thought. “A beauty, certainly, but no angel.”

Earnshaw gruffly told her to take her things into the kitchen. “Take them yourself,” she said, pushing them away as soon as she had finished. She withdrew to a stool by the window and began cutting shapes of birds and animals from the turnip peelings in her lap. Pretending I wanted to look at the garden, I approached and, very deftly I thought, dropped Mrs. Dean's note onto her knee without Hareton noticing. But she asked aloud, “What's that?” and tossed it off.

“A letter from your old friend, the housekeeper at the Grange,” I answered, annoyed that she had exposed my kindness and afraid it might be mistaken for a message of my own. On hearing this she would gladly have picked it up, but Hareton was quicker. He snatched it and put it inside his waistcoat, saying Mr. Heathcliff must see it first. Catherine silently turned away from us, slipped out her handkerchief as secretly as she could, and put it to her eyes. For a while her cousin struggled to suppress his softer feelings, then pulled out the letter and threw it on the floor beside her as ungraciously as possible. Catherine seized it and read it eagerly. She asked me a few questions about the inhabitants of her former home, human and animal, then looked towards the hills and murmured to herself:

“I wish I could ride Minny down there! I wish I could climb up there! Oh, I'm tired—I'm _fed up_, Hareton!” She leaned her pretty head against the sill with a sound halfway between a yawn and a sigh, and sank into an absent sadness, neither knowing nor caring whether we noticed her.

“Mrs. Heathcliff,” I said after sitting silently for some time, “do you realise that I know you? So well, in fact, that I'm surprised you won't come and talk to me. My housekeeper never tires of talking about you and singing your praises. She'll be terribly disappointed if I bring back no news of you, or message from you, beyond saying that you received her letter and said nothing!”
She seemed surprised by this speech and asked—
“Does Ellen like you?”
“Yes, very much,” I answered, with some hesitation.
“Then tell her,” she continued, “that I'd answer her letter, but I've nothing to write with or on. Not even a book I could tear a page from.”
“No books!” I exclaimed. “If I may ask, how do you manage to live here without them? Even with a large library, I'm often terribly bored at the Grange. Take my books away and I'd be desperate!”

“When I had them, I was always reading,” Catherine said. “Mr. Heathcliff never reads, so he took it into his head to destroy my books. I haven't seen one for weeks. Once I searched through Joseph's stock of theology, which made him furious. And once, Hareton, I found a secret collection in your room: Latin and Greek, stories and poetry, all old friends. The stories and poems were ones I'd brought here. You collected them like a magpie collecting silver spoons, simply for the pleasure of stealing! They're no use to you. Or perhaps you hid them out of spite: if you can't enjoy them, nobody else shall. Perhaps it was _your_ envy that suggested Mr. Heathcliff should rob me of my treasures? But most of them are written in my mind and printed on my heart, and you can't take those away!”
Earnshaw went crimson as his cousin exposed his private collection of books and stammered an indignant denial of her charges.
“Mr. Hareton wishes to improve his knowledge,” I said, coming to his aid. “He doesn't _envy_ your accomplishments; he wants to _equal_ them. In a few years he'll be a fine scholar.”

“And meanwhile he wants me to become a dunce,” Catherine replied. “Yes, I hear him trying to spell and read to himself. What fine mistakes he makes! I wish you'd repeat Chevy Chase the way you did yesterday. It was extremely funny. I heard you, and I heard you searching the dictionary for the difficult words, then swearing because you couldn't read the definitions!”

The young man plainly thought it unfair to be mocked for his ignorance, then mocked again for trying to overcome it. I thought much the same. Remembering Mrs. Dean's account of his first attempt to dispel the darkness in which he had been raised, I remarked, “But, Mrs. Heathcliff, we all had to begin, and we all stumbled and faltered at first. If our teachers had mocked us instead of helping, we'd still be stumbling and faltering.”

“Oh, I don't want to limit his learning,” she replied. “But he has no right to take what's mine and make it ridiculous to me with his horrible mistakes and mispronunciations! Those books, the prose and the poetry alike, are sacred to me because of other memories. I hate hearing them degraded and profaned in his mouth! And out of everything he could choose, he's picked my favourite passages, the ones I most love to repeat, as though deliberately to spite me.”

For a minute Hareton's chest heaved in silence. His humiliation and anger were intense, and he struggled to control them. With a gentleman's wish to ease his embarrassment, I got up and stood in the doorway, looking outside. He followed my example and left the room, but soon returned with half a dozen books. He flung them into Catherine's lap, exclaiming, “Take them! I never want to hear them, read them, or think of them again!”
“I don't want them now,” she answered. “They'll remind me of you, and I'll hate them.”

She opened one that had clearly been much handled and read a passage in a beginner's slow, dragging voice. Then she laughed and threw it away. “And listen to this,” she went on tauntingly, beginning a verse of an old ballad in the same manner.

But his pride could bear no more torment. I heard a blow silence her insolent tongue, and I did not entirely disapprove. The little wretch had done everything she could to wound her cousin's sensitive, though uncultivated, feelings. Physical force was the only argument he had to settle the account and return some of the hurt to the person who had inflicted it. Afterwards he gathered the books and threw them into the fire. His face showed the anguish of that sacrifice to anger. As they burned, I imagined him remembering the pleasure they had already given him, and the triumph and ever greater pleasures he had expected from them. I thought I could also guess what had prompted his secret studies. Until Catherine crossed his path, he had been content with daily labour and coarse, physical pleasures. Shame at her contempt and hope of winning her approval had first stirred him towards higher things. Instead of protecting him from the first and winning him the second, his efforts to improve himself had achieved precisely the opposite.
“Yes, that's all a brute like you can get out of them!” Catherine cried, sucking her injured lip and watching the blaze with angry eyes.
“You'd _better_ keep quiet now,” he answered fiercely.

He was too agitated to say more. He hurried towards the doorway, where I stepped aside for him. But before he had crossed the threshold, Mr. Heathcliff met him coming up the paved path, laid a hand on his shoulder, and asked, “What's the matter now, lad?”
“Nowt, nowt,” he said, breaking away to indulge his grief and anger alone.
Heathcliff watched him go and sighed.

“It would be strange if I defeated myself,” he muttered, unaware that I stood behind him. “But when I look for his father in his face, I find more of _her_ every day! How the devil can he be so like her? I can hardly bear to look at him.”

He lowered his eyes and went gloomily inside. His face had a restless, anxious expression I had never seen before, and he looked thinner. His daughter-in-law had spotted him through the window and immediately escaped to the kitchen, leaving me alone.

“I'm glad to see you out again, Mr. Lockwood,” he said in answer to my greeting. “Partly for selfish reasons. In this wilderness I don't think I could easily find someone to replace you. More than once I've wondered what brought you here.”

“An idle whim, I'm afraid, sir,” I replied. “Or else it's an idle whim that's about to carry me away. I leave for London next week, and I must warn you that I have no wish to keep Thrushcross Grange beyond the twelve months I agreed to rent it. I don't think I shall live there again.”

“Indeed! Tired of exile from the world, are you?” he said. “But if you've come to ask to be excused from paying for a house you won't occupy, you've wasted your journey. I never let anyone off what they owe me.”
“I've come to ask for no such thing!” I exclaimed, thoroughly irritated. “If you wish, I'll settle with you now.” I took my notebook from my pocket.

“No, no,” he replied coolly. “If you don't come back, you'll leave enough behind to cover your debts. I'm in no hurry. Sit down and have dinner with us. A guest who can be relied on not to return is generally welcome. Catherine! Bring the things in. Where are you?”
Catherine came back carrying a tray of knives and forks.
“You can eat with Joseph,” Heathcliff muttered to her aside, “and stay in the kitchen until he's gone.”
She followed his instructions exactly. Perhaps she felt no temptation to disobey. Living among boors and people who hate mankind, she probably cannot appreciate better company when she encounters it.

With Mr. Heathcliff grim and gloomy on one side and Hareton entirely silent on the other, I ate a rather cheerless meal and took my leave early. I would have gone out the back way for a final glimpse of Catherine and the pleasure of annoying old Joseph. But Hareton was told to bring my horse round, and my host himself escorted me to the front door, thwarting my intention.

“How drearily life passes in that house!” I reflected as I rode down the road. “What a fulfilment of something more romantic than a fairy tale it would have been for Mrs. Linton Heathcliff if she and I had fallen in love, as her good nurse wished, and gone off together into the lively atmosphere of town!”

chapters.title: Chapter XXXII
paragraphs: 1802.—This September a friend in the north invited me to help devastate the game on his moors. On my way to his house, I unexpectedly found myself within fifteen miles of Gimmerton. At a roadside inn, the stableman was holding a bucket of water for my horses when a cart passed laden with newly cut oats, still very green. “That's from Gimmerton,” he remarked. “They're always three weeks behind other folk with their harvest.”
“Gimmerton?” I repeated. My time in that neighbourhood already seemed dim and dreamlike. “Ah, yes. How far is it from here?”
“Maybe fourteen miles over t' hills,” he answered. “And a rough road.”

I suddenly felt an urge to visit Thrushcross Grange. It was barely noon, and I thought I might as well sleep under my own roof as at an inn. Besides, I could easily spare a day to settle matters with my landlord and save myself another journey into the neighbourhood. After resting a while, I told my servant to ask the way to the village. We covered the distance in about three hours, greatly tiring our horses.

I left him there and went on alone down the valley. The grey church looked greyer, the lonely churchyard lonelier. I saw a moorland sheep cropping the short grass on the graves. The weather was lovely and warm—too warm for travelling—but the heat did not spoil my pleasure in the beautiful scenery above and below. Had I seen it nearer August, I am sure it would have tempted me to idle away a month in those solitary places. Nothing could be drearier in winter, or more heavenly in summer, than those valleys enclosed by hills and those bold, steep swells of heather.

I reached the Grange before sunset and knocked. But a single thin curl of blue smoke rising from the kitchen chimney suggested that the household had withdrawn to the back, and no one heard me. I rode into the yard. A girl of nine or ten sat knitting under the porch, while an old woman reclined on the steps, thoughtfully smoking a pipe.
“Is Mrs. Dean in?” I asked the old woman.
“Mistress Dean? Nay!” she answered. “She doesn't live here. She's up at t' Heights.”
“Then are you the housekeeper?” I asked.
“Aye, I keep t' house,” she replied.
“Well, I'm Mr. Lockwood, the master. I wonder whether there's a room for me? I'd like to stay the night.”
“T' master!” she cried in amazement. “Why, who knew ye were coming? Ye should have sent word. There's nowt dry or decent about t' place—not a thing!”

She dropped her pipe and hurried inside, followed by the girl and then me. I soon saw that her description was accurate and that my unwelcome appearance had almost driven her out of her wits. I told her to calm herself. I would go for a walk; meanwhile she should try to prepare a corner of a sitting room for my supper and a bedroom for the night. There was no need to sweep or dust: a good fire and dry sheets would be enough. She seemed eager to do her best, though she thrust the hearth brush into the grate instead of the poker and put several other tools to equally unsuitable uses. I left, trusting her energy to provide somewhere to rest on my return. Wuthering Heights was my destination. Just after leaving the yard, another thought brought me back.
“Is everyone well at the Heights?” I asked her.
“Aye, for all I know!” she answered, hurrying away with a pan of hot cinders.

I wanted to ask why Mrs. Dean had left the Grange, but at such a crisis I could not detain the woman, so I turned and went. I walked at leisure, with the glow of the setting sun behind me and the gentle splendour of the rising moon ahead, one fading as the other brightened. Leaving the park, I climbed the stony side road to Mr. Heathcliff's house. Before it came into sight, all that remained of daylight was a flat amber glow in the west. Yet the magnificent moon showed every pebble in the path and every blade of grass. I had neither to climb the gate nor knock: it opened at my touch. An improvement, I thought. My nose discovered another: the fragrance of stocks and wallflowers drifted through the air from among the familiar fruit trees.

The doors and windows were open, yet a fine red fire lit the hearth, as is usual in a coal district. The comfort of the sight makes the extra heat bearable. Besides, the main room at Wuthering Heights is large enough for its occupants to sit well beyond the fire's warmth. Those present had accordingly settled near a window. Before entering I could see them and hear their conversation, and so I watched and listened, drawn by a mixture of curiosity and envy that grew the longer I lingered.
“Con-_trary_!” said a voice sweet as a silver bell. “That's the third time, you dunce! I won't tell you again. Remember, or I'll pull your hair!”
“Contrary, then,” another voice answered, deep but gentle. “Now kiss me for getting it right.”
“No. Read it through correctly first, without one mistake.”

The young man began reading. He was respectably dressed and seated at a table with a book before him. His handsome face glowed with pleasure, and his eyes kept straying impatiently from the page to a small white hand over his shoulder. Whenever its owner caught these signs of inattention, a brisk slap on his cheek brought him back to his work. She stood behind him, her bright, fair ringlets sometimes mingling with his brown hair as she bent over to guide his studies. Her face—it was fortunate he could not see her face, or he would never have stayed so attentive. I could see it, and bit my lip with resentment at having thrown away whatever chance I might once have had to do more than stare at its devastating beauty.

The lesson ended, though not without further mistakes. The pupil claimed his reward and received at least five kisses, which he generously returned. Then they came to the door. From their conversation I gathered that they meant to walk on the moors. I supposed Hareton Earnshaw would condemn me, inwardly if not aloud, to the deepest pit of hell if I showed my unfortunate face near him just then. Feeling thoroughly small and spiteful, I slunk round to seek refuge in the kitchen. That entrance was open too. By the door sat my old friend Nelly Dean, sewing and singing, though her song was repeatedly interrupted from inside by harsh expressions of contempt and intolerance delivered in a far from musical voice.

“I'd far rather have them swearing in my ears from morning till night than listen to thee at all!” said the occupant of the kitchen, answering something I had not heard Nelly say. “It's a blazing shame I can't open t' blessed Book without thee starting up those praises of Satan and all t' dreadful wickedness ever born into this world! Oh, thou's a right good-for-nowt, and so is she, and that poor lad'll be lost between ye. Poor lad!” he added with a groan. “He's bewitched, I'm certain of it. Oh, Lord, judge them, for there's neither law nor justice among our rulers!”

“No, or I suppose we'd be sitting in burning bundles of sticks,” the singer retorted. “But hush, old man. Read your Bible like a Christian and leave me alone. This is ‘Fairy Annie's Wedding,’ a lovely tune, and you can dance to it.”

Mrs. Dean was about to begin again when I stepped forward. Recognising me at once, she sprang up. “Why, bless you, Mr. Lockwood! How could you think of coming back like this? Thrushcross Grange is all shut up. You should have let us know!”
“I've arranged to stay there for as long as I need,” I replied. “I leave again tomorrow. But how did you come to be transplanted here, Mrs. Dean? Tell me that.”
“Zillah left, and soon after you went to London Mr. Heathcliff asked me to come and stay until you returned. But do come in! Have you walked from Gimmerton this evening?”
“From the Grange,” I answered. “While they make a room ready for me, I want to finish my business with your master. I don't expect another opportunity soon.”
“What business, sir?” Nelly asked, leading me inside. “He's out at the moment and won't be back for a while.”
“The rent,” I answered.
“Oh! Then you'll have to settle that with Mrs. Heathcliff,” she said, “or rather with me. She hasn't learnt to manage her affairs yet, so I act for her. There's no one else.”
I looked surprised.
“Ah, I see you haven't heard of Heathcliff's death,” she continued.
“Heathcliff dead!” I exclaimed in astonishment. “How long ago?”
“Three months. But sit down and give me your hat, and I'll tell you everything. Wait—you haven't had anything to eat, have you?”
“I don't need anything. I've ordered supper at home. Sit down yourself. I never imagined he'd die! Tell me how it happened. You say they won't be back for some time—the young people?”
“No. I have to scold them every evening for walking out so late, but they take no notice of me. At least have some of our old ale. It'll do you good; you look tired.”

She hurried to fetch it before I could refuse. I heard Joseph asking whether “it wasn't a crying scandal for her to have men following her at her age? And then to fetch those jugs out of t' master's cellar! He was fair ashamed to stand by and watch it.”

She did not pause to answer him, but returned a moment later with a silver pint mug foaming at the brim. I praised its contents with appropriate enthusiasm. Then she told me the rest of Heathcliff's story. He had come to a “queer” end, as she put it.

Within a fortnight of your departure, she said, I was summoned to Wuthering Heights, and for Catherine's sake I went gladly. My first meeting with her shocked and grieved me: she had changed so much since we parted. Mr. Heathcliff gave no reason for changing his mind about my coming. He merely said he wanted me and was tired of seeing Catherine. I was to use the little parlour as my sitting room and keep her with me. Having to see her once or twice a day was enough for him. She seemed pleased with this arrangement. Gradually I smuggled over a great many books and other things that had amused her at the Grange, and persuaded myself we would be reasonably comfortable. That illusion did not last. Catherine was content at first, but soon became irritable and restless. For one thing, she was forbidden to go beyond the garden, and as spring approached its narrow limits distressed her terribly. For another, my household duties often forced me to leave her, and she complained of loneliness. She preferred quarrelling with Joseph in the kitchen to sitting peacefully alone. I did not mind their skirmishes. But when the master wanted the main room to himself, Hareton too was often driven into the kitchen. At first she either left when he came or quietly helped with my work, avoiding any mention of him or word to him; and he remained as sullen and silent as he could. After a while, though, she changed. She could no longer leave him alone. She spoke at him, commented on his stupidity and laziness, and wondered aloud how he could bear his life—how he could spend a whole evening staring at the fire and dozing.

“He's just like a dog, isn't he, Ellen?” she said once. “Or a cart horse? He works, eats, and sleeps for ever! What an empty, dreary mind he must have! Do you ever dream, Hareton? If you do, what about? But you can't speak to me!”
She looked at him, but he would neither answer nor look back.
“Perhaps he's dreaming now,” she went on. “His shoulder twitched just like Juno's. Ask him, Ellen.”
“If you don't behave, Mr. Hareton will ask the master to send you upstairs!” I said. He had not merely twitched his shoulder; he had clenched his fist, as though tempted to use it.

“I know why Hareton never speaks when I'm in the kitchen,” she exclaimed another time. “He's afraid I'll laugh at him. Ellen, what do you think? He once started teaching himself to read, and because I laughed he burnt his books and gave it up. Wasn't that foolish?”
“And weren't you unkind?” I said. “Answer that.”
“Perhaps I was,” she continued, “but I didn't expect him to be so silly. Hareton, if I gave you a book now, would you take it? I'll try!”
She laid the book she had been reading on his hand. He flung it away and muttered that if she did not stop he would break her neck.
“Well, I'll put it here,” she said, “in the table drawer. I'm going to bed.”

She whispered that I should watch whether he touched it, then left. But he would not go near it. When I told her the next morning, she was bitterly disappointed. I could see she regretted his continuing sullenness and idleness. Her conscience reproached her for driving him away from self-improvement; she had done that thoroughly. But her ingenuity was now working to repair the harm. While I ironed or did other work that kept me in one place and could not easily be done in the parlour, she would bring an entertaining book and read aloud. If Hareton was there, she generally stopped at an interesting point and left the book lying about. She tried this repeatedly, but he was stubborn as a mule. Instead of taking the bait, in wet weather he began smoking with Joseph. They sat like two mechanical figures on opposite sides of the fire, the older man fortunately too deaf to understand her wicked nonsense, as he would have called it, and the younger doing his best to appear indifferent. On fine evenings Hareton went shooting. Catherine yawned and sighed, pestered me to talk to her, then ran into the yard or garden the moment I began. Finally she resorted to tears, saying she was tired of living and that her life was useless.

Mr. Heathcliff, increasingly averse to company, had almost entirely banished Earnshaw from his room. An accident early in March confined Hareton to the kitchen for several days. His gun burst while he was alone on the hills. A splinter cut his arm, and he lost a great deal of blood before he reached home. He was consequently forced to rest beside the fire until he recovered. Catherine liked having him there. At any rate, she hated her upstairs room more than ever and made me find jobs downstairs so she could come with me.

On Easter Monday Joseph took some cattle to Gimmerton fair. That afternoon I was busy ironing linen in the kitchen. Earnshaw sat in the chimney corner, as gloomy as ever. My little mistress passed an idle hour drawing pictures on the windowpanes, varying her amusement with subdued snatches of song, whispered exclamations, and quick, irritated, impatient glances towards her cousin. He steadily smoked and stared into the grate. When I told her I could do without her blocking my light any longer, she moved to the hearth. I paid little attention to what she was doing, but soon heard her begin: “Hareton, I've realised that I want—that I'm glad—that I'd like you to be my cousin now, if you hadn't become so cross with me and so rough.”
Hareton gave no answer.
“Hareton, Hareton, Hareton! Can you hear me?” she continued.
“Get away with ye!” he growled, utterly unyielding.
“Let me have that pipe,” she said, cautiously reaching out and taking it from his mouth.
Before he could try to recover it, she had broken it and thrown it behind the fire. He swore at her and grabbed another.
“Wait!” she cried. “You must listen first. I can't talk with those clouds floating in my face.”
“Will ye go to the devil,” he snarled, “and leave me alone!”

“No, I won't,” she persisted. “I don't know how to make you talk to me, and you're determined not to understand. When I call you stupid, I don't mean anything. I don't mean I despise you. Come, Hareton, you must take notice of me. You're my cousin, and you must acknowledge me.”

“I'll have nowt to do with thee, thy filthy pride, or thy damned mocking tricks!” he answered. “I'll go to hell, body and soul, before I so much as look thy way again. Get out of t' way, now, this minute!”
Catherine frowned and went back to the window seat, biting her lip and trying to hide her growing urge to sob by humming an odd tune.
“You ought to make friends with your cousin, Mr. Hareton,” I put in, “since she's sorry for her rudeness. It would do you a world of good. Having her for company would make a different man of you.”
“Company!” he cried. “When she hates me and doesn't think me fit to wipe her shoes! Nay, even if it made me a king, I won't be scorned again for trying to please her.”
“I'm not the one who hates you—you hate me!” Cathy wept, no longer hiding her distress. “You hate me as much as Mr. Heathcliff does, and more.”

“Thou's a damned liar,” Earnshaw began. “Then why have I angered him a hundred times by taking thy side? Even when thou sneered at me and despised me, and—Keep plaguing me, and I'll go in there and tell him thou's worried me out of the kitchen!”
“I didn't know you'd taken my side,” she answered, drying her eyes. “I was miserable and bitter towards everyone. But now I thank you and ask you to forgive me. What more can I do?”

She came back to the hearth and openly held out her hand. He scowled darkly as a thundercloud, keeping his fists tightly closed and his eyes on the floor. Catherine must instinctively have understood that stubborn perversity, rather than dislike, lay behind his behaviour. After hesitating a moment, she bent and gently kissed his cheek. The little rogue thought I had not seen. She drew back and returned quite demurely to the window. I shook my head at her in reproach. She blushed and whispered, “Well, what else could I do, Ellen? He wouldn't shake hands or look at me. I had to show him somehow that I like him and want to be friends.”
I cannot say whether the kiss persuaded Hareton. For several minutes he took great care to hide his face, and when he finally raised it, he seemed desperately uncertain where to look.
Catherine neatly wrapped a handsome book in white paper, tied it with a ribbon, and addressed it to “Mr. Hareton Earnshaw.” Then she asked me to act as her ambassador and deliver the present.
“Tell him that if he'll accept it, I'll come and teach him to read it properly,” she said. “If he refuses, I'll go upstairs and never bother him again.”

I carried it over and repeated the message, anxiously watched by the person who had sent me. Hareton would not unclench his fingers, so I put it on his knee. He did not knock it off. I went back to my work. Catherine rested her head and arms on the table until she heard the faint rustle of the paper being removed. Then she slipped away and quietly sat beside her cousin. He trembled and blushed. All his rudeness and sullen harshness had left him. At first he could not find the courage to answer her questioning look or whispered plea.
“Say you forgive me, Hareton. Please. That one little word would make me so happy.”
He muttered something I could not hear.
“And will you be my friend?” Catherine asked.
“Nay, thou'll be ashamed of me every day of thy life,” he answered, “and the better thou knows me, the more ashamed thou'll be. I can't bear it.”
“So you won't be my friend?” she said, smiling sweetly and edging closer.

I could make out no more of their conversation. But when I looked round again, two such radiant faces were bent over the accepted book that I had no doubt both sides had agreed to peace. From that moment, the enemies were sworn allies.

The book was full of expensive illustrations. These, and their situation, charmed them enough to keep them in their seats until Joseph returned. The poor man was appalled to see Catherine sitting on the same bench as Hareton Earnshaw, with her hand on his shoulder, and bewildered that his favourite tolerated her closeness. He was too deeply affected to comment that night. His feelings showed only in the immense sighs he gave as he solemnly opened his large Bible on the table and covered it with dirty banknotes from his pocketbook, the proceeds of the day's business. Finally he called Hareton away.
“Take these in to t' master, lad,” he said, “and stay there. I'm going up to my own room. This hole's neither decent nor fit for us. We must clear out and find another.”
“Come, Catherine,” I said, “we must ‘clear out’ too. I've finished ironing. Are you ready?”
“It isn't eight yet!” she answered, reluctantly getting up. “Hareton, I'll leave this book on the mantelpiece and bring some more tomorrow.”
“Any books thou leaves here, I'll take into t' main room,” Joseph said, “and thou'll be lucky to find them again. So please thysen!”

Cathy threatened that his library would pay for hers. Smiling at Hareton as she passed, she went upstairs singing, lighter-hearted, I venture to say, than she had ever been under that roof, except perhaps on her earliest visits to Linton.

The friendship that began this way grew quickly, though it suffered occasional interruptions. Earnshaw could not be made polished simply by wishing it, and my young mistress was no philosopher or model of patience. But their minds were moving towards the same end: one loved and wanted to respect, the other loved and wanted to be respected. In time they managed to reach it.

You see, Mr. Lockwood, winning Mrs. Heathcliff's heart was easy enough. But now I'm glad you didn't try. The marriage of those two will fulfil all my wishes. On their wedding day I shall envy nobody. There won't be a happier woman in England!

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIII
paragraphs: The next day, Tuesday, Earnshaw was still unable to return to his usual work and remained around the house. I soon discovered that keeping my charge beside me as before was now impossible. She went downstairs ahead of me and out into the garden, where she had seen her cousin doing some light work. When I went to call them to breakfast, I found she had persuaded him to clear a large patch of currant and gooseberry bushes. They were busy planning which plants to bring over from the Grange.
The destruction they had managed in a mere half-hour horrified me. Those blackcurrant bushes were Joseph's pride and joy, and she had chosen the very middle of them for a flower bed.

“There! The master will hear about all this the moment it's discovered,” I exclaimed. “What excuse can you offer for taking such liberties with the garden? There'll be a fine explosion over it, just you wait! Mr. Hareton, I'm surprised you haven't more sense than to make such a mess at her bidding!”
“I forgot they were Joseph's,” Earnshaw answered, looking rather disconcerted. “But I'll tell him I did it.”

We always ate with Mr. Heathcliff. I performed the mistress's duties of making tea and carving, so I was needed at the table. Catherine usually sat beside me, but that morning she edged closer to Hareton. I soon saw that she would be no more discreet in friendship than she had been in hostility.
“Mind you don't talk to your cousin too much or pay him too much attention,” I whispered as we entered. “It will certainly annoy Mr. Heathcliff, and he'll be angry with both of you.”
“I won't,” she answered.
A minute later she had sidled up to Hareton and was putting primroses in his porridge.

He dared not speak to her there, scarcely even look at her. Yet she kept teasing until twice she almost made him laugh. I frowned, and she glanced towards the master, whose face showed that his mind was occupied with something quite apart from his companions. For a moment she grew serious and studied him intently. Then she turned back to her nonsense, until at last Hareton gave a stifled laugh. Mr. Heathcliff started and looked quickly from face to face. Catherine met his eyes with that mixture of nervousness and defiance which he hated.

“It's just as well you're out of my reach!” he exclaimed. “What devil possesses you to keep staring back at me with those infernal eyes? Lower them! Don't remind me you're here again. I thought I'd cured you of laughing.”
“It was me,” Hareton muttered.
“What did you say?” the master demanded.

Hareton looked down at his plate and did not repeat his confession. Mr. Heathcliff watched him a moment, then silently returned to his breakfast and his interrupted thoughts. We had almost finished. The two young people wisely moved farther apart, and I expected no more trouble during the meal. Then Joseph appeared in the doorway. His trembling lip and furious eyes showed that he had discovered the outrage against his precious bushes. He must have seen Cathy and her cousin there before inspecting the damage. His jaws worked like a cow chewing its cud, making his words difficult to understand as he began:

“I must have my wages, and I must go! I'd _meant_ to die where I've served for sixty years. I thought I'd carry my books and all my bits o' things up to t' attic and let them have t' kitchen to themselves, for peace's sake. It was hard to give up my own hearth, but I thought I _could_ do that! Now she's taken my garden, and by my heart, master, I can't stand it! Thou can bend to t' yoke if thou likes. I'm not used to it, and an old man doesn't soon take to new burdens. I'd sooner earn my bread and drink breaking stones on t' road!”
“Now, now, you idiot!” Heathcliff interrupted. “Make it short. What's your grievance? I won't interfere in quarrels between you and Nelly. She can shut you in the coal cellar for all I care.”

“It's not Nelly!” Joseph answered. “I wouldn't leave for Nelly, nasty good-for-nowt though she is. Thank God _she_ can't steal anybody's soul! She's never been so handsome a body couldn't look at her without blinking. It's yon dreadful, graceless hussy who's bewitched our lad with her bold eyes and forward ways, till—Nay, it fair breaks my heart! He's forgotten all I've done for him, all I've made of him, and gone and torn up a whole row of t' finest currant bushes in t' garden!” At that he broke into open lamentation, overcome by the bitterness of his injuries and by Earnshaw's ingratitude and dangerous state.
“Is the fool drunk?” Mr. Heathcliff asked. “Hareton, is it you he's complaining about?”
“I've pulled up two or three bushes,” the young man replied, “but I'll plant them again.”
“Why did you pull them up?” the master asked.
Catherine thought it wise to put in a word.
“We wanted to plant flowers there,” she cried. “It's entirely my fault. I asked him to do it.”
“And who the devil gave _you_ permission to touch a stick in this place?” her father-in-law demanded, much astonished. Turning to Hareton, he added, “And who told _you_ to obey her?”
Hareton could not speak. His cousin answered, “You shouldn't begrudge me a few yards of earth to make pretty when you've taken all my land!”
“Your land, you insolent slut! You never had any,” Heathcliff said.
“And my money,” she went on, returning his angry stare while biting the last crust of her breakfast.
“Silence!” he cried. “Finish and get out!”
“And Hareton's land and money,” the reckless girl continued. “Hareton and I are friends now, and I'm going to tell him everything about you!”
For a moment the master seemed stunned. He went pale and stood, never taking his eyes from her, with a look of deadly hatred.
“If you hit me, Hareton will hit you,” she said. “So you might as well sit down.”

“If Hareton doesn't throw you out, I'll knock him straight to hell!” Heathcliff thundered. “Damned witch! Do you dare try to turn him against me? Get her out! Do you hear? Throw her into the kitchen! Ellen Dean, if you let her come in my sight again, I'll kill her!”
Under his breath, Hareton tried to persuade her to leave.
“Drag her away!” Heathcliff shouted savagely. “Are you standing there talking?” He came forward to carry out the order himself.
“He won't obey you any more, you wicked man,” Catherine said. “And soon he'll hate you as much as I do.”
“Hush, hush!” the young man muttered reproachfully. “I won't hear thee speak to him like that. Stop it.”
“But you won't let him hit me?” she cried.
“Then come away,” he whispered urgently.
It was too late. Heathcliff had seized her.
“Now _you_ go!” he told Earnshaw. “Accursed witch! This time she's provoked me when I couldn't bear it. I'll make her regret it for the rest of her life!”

His hand was tangled in her hair. Hareton tried to loosen his grip, begging him not to hurt her this once. Heathcliff's dark eyes blazed. He looked ready to tear Catherine apart, and I had just worked myself up to risk rescuing her when suddenly his fingers loosened. He moved his grip from her hair to her arm and stared intently into her face. Then he passed a hand over his eyes and stood a moment, apparently collecting himself. Turning back to Catherine, he said with forced calm, “You must learn not to drive me into a rage, or one day I really will murder you! Go with Mrs. Dean and stay with her. Let her be the only one who hears your insolence. As for Hareton Earnshaw, if I see him listening to you, I'll send him out to find his bread where he can. Your love will make him an outcast and a beggar. Nelly, take her away. Leave me, all of you! Leave me!”

I led my young mistress out. She was too glad to escape to resist. Hareton followed, leaving Mr. Heathcliff alone until dinner. I had advised Catherine to eat upstairs, but when he saw her empty place he sent me to fetch her. He spoke to none of us, ate very little, and went out directly afterwards, saying he would not return until evening.

While he was away, the two new friends settled in the main room. There I heard Hareton sharply stop his cousin when she offered to explain how her father-in-law had treated his father. He would not allow a word against him, he said. Even if Heathcliff were the devil, it made no difference: he would stand by him. He would rather she abused him as she used to than attack Mr. Heathcliff. Catherine was growing angry, but he found a way to silence her by asking how she would like _him_ to speak badly of her father. Then she understood that Earnshaw felt the master's reputation as his own, and was attached to him by bonds stronger than reason could break—chains forged by habit, which it would be cruel to try to loosen. Afterwards she showed her good heart by avoiding both complaints about Heathcliff and expressions of hatred. She told me she was sorry she had tried to set him and Hareton against each other. Indeed, I don't believe she has spoken a single word against her oppressor in Hareton's hearing since.

Once this small disagreement ended, they were friends again and completely absorbed in their roles of pupil and teacher. When my work was done, I went to sit with them. Watching them gave me such peace and comfort that I lost all sense of time. You see, I felt they were both my children in a way. I had long been proud of one, and now I was sure the other would make me just as happy. His honest, warm, intelligent nature was rapidly shaking off the ignorance and degradation in which it had been raised. Catherine's genuine praise drove him to work harder. As his mind brightened, so did his face, gaining life and dignity. I could scarcely believe he was the same person I had seen when I found my little mistress at Wuthering Heights after her expedition to the Crags. While I watched with admiration and they worked, dusk fell, and the master returned. He came upon us quite unexpectedly through the front door and saw all three of us before we could raise our heads. Well, I thought, there could be no pleasanter or more innocent sight. Scolding them would be shameful. The red firelight shone on their two lovely heads and showed their faces alive with the eager interest of children. Though he was twenty-three and she eighteen, both had so much new to feel and learn that neither felt or displayed the sobriety of disenchanted adulthood.

They looked up together at Mr. Heathcliff. Perhaps you have never noticed that their eyes are exactly alike, and that they are Catherine Earnshaw's eyes. The younger Catherine has no other resemblance to her, apart from a broad forehead and a certain curve of the nostril that makes her look rather proud whether she means to or not. In Hareton the resemblance goes further. It is remarkable at any time, but _then_ it was especially striking, because his senses were keen and his mind was unusually awake and active. I suppose that likeness disarmed Mr. Heathcliff. He walked towards the hearth, visibly agitated, but the agitation quickly subsided as he looked at the young man—or rather changed its character, for it was still there. He took the book from Hareton's hand, glanced at the open page, and returned it without comment. He merely motioned Catherine away. Her companion followed almost immediately. I too was about to go, but he told me to stay seated.

“A poor ending, isn't it?” he said, after dwelling for a while on what he had just seen. “An absurd conclusion to all my violent efforts? I gather levers and pickaxes to demolish both houses. I train myself to work like Hercules. Then, when everything is ready and within my power, I find I haven't the will to lift one slate from either roof! My old enemies haven't beaten me. Now would be exactly the time to revenge myself on those who stand in their place. I could do it, and no one could stop me. But what's the point? I no longer care to strike. I can't be bothered to raise my hand! That makes it sound as though I've worked all this time merely to display some splendid generosity. Nothing could be further from the truth. I've lost the ability to enjoy their destruction, and I'm too idle to destroy them for nothing.

“Nelly, a strange change is coming. I'm in its shadow now. My daily life interests me so little that I hardly remember to eat or drink. Those two who just left are the only things that still seem solid and distinct to me, and the sight of them hurts almost beyond endurance. I won't speak about _her_, and I don't want to think about her. I earnestly wish she were invisible: her presence rouses nothing but feelings that drive me mad. _He_ affects me differently. Yet if I could avoid ever seeing him again without appearing insane, I would! Perhaps you'll think I'm heading that way,” he added, trying to smile, “if I describe the thousand memories and ideas he awakens or embodies. But you won't repeat what I tell you. My mind has been shut up inside itself so endlessly that at last it's tempting to open it to someone else.

“Five minutes ago Hareton seemed the embodiment of my youth, not a human being. I felt so many different things towards him that I couldn't possibly have spoken to him rationally. First, his astonishing likeness to Catherine bound him to her in a terrible way. You might think that was what most powerfully seized my imagination, but it is actually the least of it. What _isn't_ connected with her for me? What doesn't remind me of her? I can't look at this floor without seeing her features formed in the flagstones! In every cloud and every tree, filling the air at night and glimpsed in every object by day, her image surrounds me! The most ordinary faces of men and women—even my own face—mock me with a resemblance. The whole world is a dreadful collection of reminders that she existed and I have lost her! Well, in Hareton's face I saw the ghost of my undying love, my wild struggles to hold on to what was mine, my degradation, my pride, my happiness, my anguish—

“But it's madness to repeat these thoughts to you. It only explains why, though I dislike always being alone, his company does me no good. It worsens the constant torment I live with. That's partly why I no longer care how he and his cousin get on together. I can't pay them any more attention.”

“But what do you mean by a _change_, Mr. Heathcliff?” I asked, alarmed by his manner. In my judgment, however, he was neither about to lose his mind nor to die. He was perfectly strong and healthy. As for his sanity, he had taken pleasure since childhood in brooding over dark things and entertaining strange fancies. He might have an obsessive madness concerning the idol he had lost, but on every other subject his mind was as sound as mine.
“I won't know until it comes,” he said. “I'm only half aware of it now.”
“You don't feel ill, do you?” I asked.
“No, Nelly, I don't,” he answered.
“Then you're not afraid of dying?” I continued.

“Afraid? No!” he replied. “I neither fear death nor foresee it nor hope for it. Why should I? With my strong constitution, moderate habits, and harmless occupations, I ought to remain above ground until there's hardly a black hair left on my head, and probably _will_. Yet I can't go on like this! I have to remind myself to breathe, almost remind my heart to beat! It's like forcing back a stiff spring. I must compel myself to make the slightest movement that doesn't spring from one thought, or to notice anything, living or dead, unconnected with that one all-embracing idea. I have a single wish. My entire being, all my powers, yearn to fulfil it. They've yearned for it so long and so steadily that I'm certain it _will_ be fulfilled, and _soon_, because it has consumed my life. I'm swallowed up in anticipating it. Confessing hasn't relieved me, but perhaps it explains some otherwise inexplicable moods of mine. O God! It's a long struggle. I wish it were over!”

He began pacing the room and muttering dreadful things to himself. I was almost persuaded, as he said Joseph had been, that his conscience had turned his heart into a hell on earth. I wondered greatly how it would end. Though he had seldom revealed this state of mind before, even in his expression, I had no doubt it was his usual condition. He said so himself. Yet no one could have guessed it from his ordinary behaviour. You didn't, Mr. Lockwood, when you met him. At the time I'm describing he was just as he was then, only more inclined to long periods alone and perhaps even less talkative in company.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIV
paragraphs: For several days after that evening, Mr. Heathcliff avoided joining us at meals, though he would not officially exclude Hareton and Cathy. He disliked giving in to his feelings so completely and preferred to stay away himself. Eating once in twenty-four hours seemed enough to sustain him.

One night, after everyone had gone to bed, I heard him go downstairs and out through the front door. I did not hear him return, and in the morning he was still absent. It was April then. The weather was gentle and warm, the grass as green as sun and showers could make it, and the two dwarf apple trees by the south wall were covered in blossom. After breakfast Catherine insisted that I bring a chair and sit with my work under the fir trees at the end of the house. She coaxed Hareton, now fully recovered from his accident, into digging and arranging her little garden, which Joseph's complaints had caused to be moved to that corner. I was comfortably enjoying the spring fragrance around me and the soft blue beauty overhead when my young mistress returned. She had run down towards the gate to gather primrose roots for a border, but came back with only half a load and told us Mr. Heathcliff was coming. “And he spoke to me,” she added, looking puzzled.
“What did he say?” Hareton asked.
“He told me to be off as quickly as I could,” she answered. “But he looked so unlike himself that I stopped for a moment to stare.”
“In what way?” he asked.
“Almost bright and cheerful. No, not _almost_ anything—_very_ excited, wild, and happy!” she replied.

“Then walking at night must amuse him,” I remarked, pretending indifference. In fact I was as surprised as she was and eager to see whether her report was true. A happy-looking master would be no everyday sight. I invented a reason to go inside. Heathcliff stood in the open doorway, pale and trembling. Yet there certainly was a strange, joyful glitter in his eyes that changed his whole face.
“Would you like some breakfast?” I asked. “You must be hungry after wandering about all night!” I wanted to find out where he had been, but did not like to ask directly.
“No, I'm not hungry,” he answered, turning his head away and speaking with some contempt, as though he guessed I was trying to discover the reason for his good mood.
I was puzzled and wondered whether this might be a suitable moment for a little advice.

“I don't think you should be roaming outdoors when you ought to be in bed,” I said. “At any rate, it's unwise in this damp season. You'll probably catch a bad cold or a fever. There's something wrong with you already!”
“Nothing I can't bear,” he answered, “and with the greatest pleasure, provided you leave me alone. Go inside and stop bothering me.”
I obeyed. As I passed, I noticed that he was breathing as rapidly as a cat.
“Yes,” I thought, “we're going to have an illness. I can't imagine what he's been doing.”
At noon he sat down to dinner with us and accepted a plate piled high with food, as though he meant to make up for his earlier fasting.
“I have neither a cold nor a fever, Nelly,” he said, referring to my morning's remark. “And I'm ready to do justice to the food you've given me.”

He picked up his knife and fork and was about to eat when his appetite seemed suddenly to vanish. He set them down, looked eagerly towards the window, then rose and went out. While we finished, we could see him pacing the garden. Earnshaw said he would go and ask why he would not eat. He thought we must somehow have upset him.
“Well, is he coming?” Catherine called when her cousin returned.

“Nay,” he answered, “but he's not angry. He seemed wonderfully pleased, in fact. I only made him impatient by speaking twice. Then he told me to go back to thee. He wondered how I could want anyone else's company.”

I put his plate on the fender to keep warm. An hour or two later, when the room was empty, he returned, no calmer than before. There was the same unnatural joy beneath his dark brows—and it _was_ unnatural—the same bloodless colour, with his teeth showing now and then in a kind of smile. His body shook, not with cold or weakness, but like a tightly stretched cord vibrating: a powerful quivering rather than a tremble.
I must ask what's wrong, I thought. Who else will? “Have you had some good news, Mr. Heathcliff?” I exclaimed. “You look unusually lively.”
“Where would good news come from for me?” he said. “It's hunger that makes me lively, and apparently I'm not to eat.”
“Your dinner is here,” I answered. “Why won't you have it?”

“I don't want it now,” he muttered quickly. “I'll wait until supper. And, Nelly, let me ask you once and for all to keep Hareton and the other one away from me. I want nobody troubling me. I want this place to myself.”
“Is there some new reason for banishing us?” I asked. “Tell me why you're behaving so strangely, Mr. Heathcliff. Where were you last night? I'm not asking out of idle curiosity, but—”

“You're asking out of very idle curiosity,” he interrupted with a laugh. “Still, I'll answer. Last night I stood at the threshold of hell. Today I can see my heaven. My eyes are fixed on it, scarcely three feet away! Now you'd better go. If you don't pry, you'll neither see nor hear anything to frighten you.”
I swept the hearth, wiped the table, and left, more bewildered than ever.

He stayed indoors for the rest of the afternoon, and no one disturbed him. At eight, though he had not called, I thought I should take in a candle and his supper. He was leaning against an open window ledge, but not looking outside: his face was turned towards the dark interior. The fire had dwindled to ashes. The damp, mild air of the cloudy evening filled the room. It was so quiet that I could hear not only the murmur of the stream down in Gimmerton, but its rippling and gurgling over pebbles and between the larger stones it could not cover. I exclaimed at the miserable state of the grate and began closing the windows one by one until I reached his.
“Shall I close this one?” I asked, trying to rouse him, for he had not moved.

As I spoke, the light flashed over his face. Oh, Mr. Lockwood, I cannot tell you what a fright that momentary glimpse gave me! Those deep, dark eyes, that smile, that deathly pallor! He looked to me like a goblin rather than Mr. Heathcliff. In my terror I tilted the candle towards the wall, and it went out, leaving me in darkness.
“Yes, close it,” he answered in his usual voice. “There, that's sheer clumsiness! Why were you holding the candle sideways? Hurry up and fetch another.”
I rushed out, foolishly terrified, and told Joseph, “The master wants you to take him a light and get the fire going.” Just then I dared not go back myself.

Joseph rattled some burning coals into a shovel and went in, but immediately returned, carrying the supper tray in his other hand. Mr. Heathcliff was going to bed, he explained, and wanted nothing to eat until morning. We heard him climb the stairs at once. He did not go to his usual room, but into the one with the enclosed bed. As I mentioned, its window is wide enough for anyone to climb through. I suspected he was planning another midnight outing and preferred us not to know.

“Is he a ghoul or a vampire?” I wondered. I had read of such hideous demons in bodily form. Then I reminded myself that I had cared for him as a child, watched him grow into youth, and followed almost his whole life. How absurd to give way to such horror! “But where did he come from, that little dark creature whom a good man sheltered to his own ruin?” superstition whispered as I drifted towards sleep. Half dreaming, I exhausted myself inventing a suitable parentage for him. Repeating my waking thoughts, I retraced his life with grim variations, finally imagining his death and funeral. All I remember of that is my great annoyance at being responsible for an inscription on his monument and consulting the sexton about it. Since he had no surname and we did not know his age, we had to content ourselves with the single word “Heathcliff.” That part came true. We did. If you go into the churchyard, you will find only that on his headstone, with the date of his death.

Daybreak brought back my common sense. As soon as there was enough light, I got up and went into the garden to look for footprints beneath his window. There were none. “He's stayed at home,” I thought, “and he'll be all right today.” I made breakfast as usual, but told Hareton and Catherine to eat before the master came down, since he was sleeping late. They preferred to take it outside beneath the trees, and I set out a little table for them.

When I came back, Mr. Heathcliff was downstairs. He and Joseph were discussing farm business. His instructions were clear and detailed, but he spoke rapidly and kept turning his head aside. His expression was as excited as before, even more so. Once Joseph left, he took his usual seat, and I put a bowl of coffee in front of him. He drew it closer, then rested his arms on the table and looked at what I thought was the opposite wall. His glittering, restless eyes travelled up and down one particular part of it with such intense interest that he stopped breathing for half a minute at a time.
“Come now,” I said, pushing some bread against his hand. “Eat and drink while it's hot. It's been waiting almost an hour.”
He took no notice, yet he smiled. I would rather have seen him grind his teeth than smile that way.
“Mr. Heathcliff! Master!” I cried. “For God's sake, don't stare as though you're seeing something from another world!”
“For God's sake, don't shout so loudly,” he replied. “Turn round and tell me: are we alone?”
“Of course,” I answered. “Of course we are.”
Even so, I found myself obeying, as though I were not quite certain. With a sweep of his hand he cleared a space among the breakfast things and leaned forward to look more freely.

Now I realised he was not looking at the wall. Watching only him, I could see he seemed to be gazing at something less than two yards away. Whatever it was apparently gave him pleasure and pain in their most intense extremes. At least, that was what his anguished yet ecstatic expression suggested. Nor did this imagined object stay still. His eyes followed it tirelessly and never left it, even when he spoke to me. I reminded him in vain how long he had gone without food. If my pleas moved him to reach for anything, if he stretched out a hand for bread, his fingers closed before reaching it and stayed on the table, their purpose forgotten.

I sat with exemplary patience, trying to draw his absorbed attention away from whatever held it. At last he became irritable and got up, asking why I would not let him take his meals in his own time. Next time, he said, I need not wait: I could set out the food and go. Then he left the house, wandered slowly down the garden path, and disappeared through the gate.

The hours dragged by in anxiety, and another evening came. I went to bed late, and even then could not sleep. He returned after midnight and, instead of going upstairs, shut himself in the room below. I listened and tossed about. At last I dressed and went down. Lying there, tormenting myself with a hundred groundless fears, was more than I could bear.

I could hear Mr. Heathcliff pacing restlessly, often breaking the silence with a deep breath that sounded like a groan. He muttered disconnected words too. The only one I could make out was Catherine's name, joined to some wild expression of love or suffering. He spoke as if to someone present, quietly and earnestly, with words wrung from the depths of his soul. I had not the courage to walk straight in, but wanted to draw him out of his trance, so I attacked the kitchen fire, stirring it and scraping the cinders. It brought him out sooner than I expected. He opened the door at once and said, “Nelly, come here. Is it morning? Bring your light in.”
“It's striking four,” I answered. “If you want a candle to take upstairs, you could have lit one at this fire.”
“No, I don't want to go upstairs,” he said. “Come in and make a fire for _me_. Do whatever needs doing in the room.”
“I must blow these coals red before I can carry any in,” I replied, fetching a chair and the bellows.
Meanwhile he wandered backwards and forwards, almost distracted, his heavy sighs coming so rapidly that there was hardly room for an ordinary breath between them.

“When it's light I'll send for Green,” he said. “I want to ask him some legal questions while I can still give those matters a thought and act calmly. I haven't made my will, and I can't decide how to leave my property. I wish I could wipe it from the face of the earth.”

“I wouldn't talk like that, Mr. Heathcliff,” I interrupted. “Let your will wait. You'll live to repent of your many injustices yet!
