I never thought your nerves would become unsettled, but they're terribly disturbed now, almost entirely through your own fault. The way you've lived these past three days could exhaust a Titan. Please eat something and get some rest. A look in the mirror would show you how much you need both. Your cheeks are hollow and your eyes bloodshot, like someone starving from hunger and going blind for lack of sleep.”

“It isn't my fault that I can't eat or rest,” he replied. “I assure you it's not deliberate. I'll do both as soon as I possibly can. But you might as well tell a man struggling in the water within arm's reach of the shore to rest! I must reach it first. Then I'll rest. Well, forget Mr. Green. As for repenting of my injustices, I've done no injustice, and I regret nothing. I'm too happy, and yet not happy enough. My soul's bliss is killing my body without satisfying itself.”
“Happy, master?” I cried. “A strange happiness! If you could listen without getting angry, I might offer some advice that would make you happier.”
“What advice?” he asked. “Tell me.”

“You know, Mr. Heathcliff,” I said, “that since you were thirteen you've lived selfishly, without Christian principles. You have probably hardly held a Bible in all that time. You must have forgotten what's in it, and perhaps you haven't time to examine it now. Could it hurt to send for someone—a minister of any denomination, it doesn't matter which—to explain it? He could show how far you've strayed from its teachings and how unfit you'll be for its heaven unless you change before you die.”

“I'm grateful rather than angry, Nelly,” he said, “because you've reminded me how I want to be buried. Have me carried to the churchyard in the evening. You and Hareton may come if you like. Above all, make sure the sexton follows my instructions about the two coffins! No minister need attend, and nothing need be said over me. I tell you, I've almost reached _my_ heaven. Other people's heaven has no value for me, and I have no desire for it.”
“And suppose you persist in this stubborn fast and die of it, and they refuse to bury you in the churchyard?” I asked, appalled by his godless indifference. “How would you like that?”
“They won't,” he replied. “If they do, you must have me moved secretly. Neglect it, and you'll have practical proof that the dead aren't annihilated!”

As soon as he heard the others stirring, he withdrew to his den, and I breathed more freely. But that afternoon, while Joseph and Hareton were at work, he came back into the kitchen. With a wild look, he told me to sit with him in the main room: he wanted company. I refused, telling him plainly that his strange words and behaviour frightened me, and I had neither the courage nor the wish to be alone with him.

“I believe you think I'm a fiend,” he said with his dismal laugh, “something too horrible to live under a respectable roof.” Then he turned to Catherine, who was there and had moved behind me when he approached. Half mockingly, he added, “Will _you_ come, pet? I won't hurt you. No! To you I've made myself worse than the devil. Well, there's _one_ who won't shrink from my company! By God, she's relentless. Oh, damn it! It's more than flesh and blood can possibly bear—even mine.”

He asked no one else for company. At dusk he went to his bedroom. All night and far into the morning we heard him groaning and murmuring to himself. Hareton wanted to go in, but I told him to fetch Mr. Kenneth, who should see him instead. When the doctor arrived, I asked to be admitted and tried the door, but it was locked. Heathcliff told us to go to hell. He was better and insisted on being left alone, so the doctor went away.

The next evening was very wet. Rain poured down until dawn. As I took my morning walk around the house, I saw the master's window swinging open and the rain driving straight inside. He can't be in bed, I thought: those showers would soak him through. He must be up or out. But I won't fuss any more. I'll go boldly in and look.

I got into the room with another key. Finding it empty, I hurried to open the panels of the bed. I pushed them aside and looked in. Mr. Heathcliff lay on his back. His eyes met mine so sharply and fiercely that I started, and then he seemed to smile. I could not believe him dead. But rain washed his face and throat, the bedclothes were dripping, and he was utterly still. The window, swinging backwards and forwards, had scraped one hand resting on the sill. No blood came from the broken skin. When I touched it, there could be no more doubt: he was dead and stiff!

I fastened the window, combed his long black hair back from his forehead, and tried to close his eyes. If possible, I wanted to extinguish that dreadful, lifelike stare of triumph before anyone else saw it. They would not close. They seemed to mock my efforts, and his parted lips and sharp white teeth mocked them too! Seized by another fit of cowardice, I called out for Joseph. He shuffled up and exclaimed, but absolutely refused to touch him.

“T' devil's carried off his soul,” he cried, “and he can have his carcass into t' bargain, for all I care! Ech! What a wicked one he looks, grinning at death!” The old sinner grinned back in mockery. I thought he meant to dance round the bed, but he suddenly composed himself, fell to his knees, raised his hands, and gave thanks that the rightful master and the old family had been restored to their rights.

The terrible event left me stunned, and my thoughts inevitably returned to earlier days with a heavy sadness. But poor Hareton, who had suffered the greatest wrong, was the only one who truly grieved deeply. He sat beside the body all night, crying bitterly. He held its hand and kissed the savage, mocking face everyone else shrank from looking at. His grief had the strength that comes naturally from a generous heart, even one as tough as tempered steel.

Mr. Kenneth could not determine what illness had killed the master. I concealed the fact that he had swallowed nothing for four days, afraid it might cause trouble. Besides, I am convinced he had not refused food deliberately. His fasting was the result of his strange illness, not its cause.

To the scandal of the whole neighbourhood, we buried him as he had asked. Earnshaw and I, the sexton, and six men to carry the coffin were the only people present. After lowering it into the grave, the six men left. We stayed to see it covered. With tears streaming down his face, Hareton dug squares of green turf and laid them himself over the brown earth. Now the grave is as smooth and green as the mounds beside it, and I hope its occupant sleeps as soundly. But ask the country people, and they would swear on the Bible that he _walks_. Some claim to have met him near the church, on the moor, even inside this house. Idle stories, you'll say, and I agree. Yet that old man by the kitchen fire insists he's seen two of them looking out of the master's bedroom window every rainy night since his death. And about a month ago something strange happened to me. I was going to the Grange one evening—a dark evening with thunder threatening—when, just at the turn by the Heights, I met a little boy driving a sheep and two lambs. He was crying terribly. I supposed the lambs were skittish and wouldn't go where he wanted.
“What's wrong, my little man?” I asked.
“Heathcliff and a woman are over there, under t' crag,” he sobbed. “I daren't go past them.”

I saw nothing. But neither he nor the sheep would go on, so I told him to take the lower road. He had probably imagined the phantoms while crossing the moors alone and thinking about the nonsense he had heard from his parents and companions. Still, I no longer like being out after dark, or being left alone in this grim house. I can't help it. I shall be glad when they leave and move to the Grange.
“So they're going to the Grange?” I asked.
“Yes,” Mrs. Dean answered, “as soon as they're married, which will be on New Year's Day.”
“Who will live here, then?”
“Joseph will look after the house, perhaps with a boy to keep him company. They'll live in the kitchen, and the rest will be closed up.”
“For whatever ghosts choose to occupy it?” I remarked.
“No, Mr. Lockwood,” Nelly said, shaking her head. “I believe the dead are at peace. But we shouldn't speak lightly of them.”
Just then the garden gate swung shut. The walkers were coming back.
“_They're_ afraid of nothing,” I grumbled, watching them approach through the window. “Together they'd face Satan and all his armies.”

As they reached the doorstep and paused for a last look at the moon—or, more accurately, at each other in its light—I felt an irresistible urge to escape them again. I pressed a small gift into Mrs. Dean's hand and ignored her protests at my rudeness. As they opened the front door, I disappeared through the kitchen. I would thus have confirmed Joseph's suspicions of his fellow servant's frivolous misconduct, had the pleasant ring of a sovereign at his feet not fortunately persuaded him that I was a respectable person.

I lengthened my walk home by turning towards the church. Beneath its walls I saw that decay had advanced even in seven months. Many windows had black gaps where the glass was gone, and here and there slates projected beyond the roofline, waiting to be loosened further by the coming autumn storms.

I looked for, and soon found, the three headstones on the slope beside the moor. The middle one was grey and half buried in heather. Turf and moss creeping around the foot of Edgar Linton's had only begun to blend it into the landscape. Heathcliff's was still bare.

I lingered beside them under that gentle sky, watching moths flutter among the heather and harebells, listening to the soft wind breathe through the grass, and wondering how anyone could imagine restless sleep for those lying in such quiet earth.
